cia-0000119202:
From February 1971, this CIA document deals with reward leaflets about American prisoners of war held in Laos. Part of the heading was deleted before release, so the person or office it was filed under is unknown. The leaflets offered money for news about captured Americans.

Leaflet rewards were one of the few tools Washington had for finding men lost in Laos. Local people who saw a prisoner, a camp, or a grave could be paid for reporting it. The document keeps the paper trail of that effort, showing how the search for prisoners ran through printed offers dropped and posted across the countryside.
cia-0000124302: A January 1958 CIA report presents orbital data on Soviet Sputniks One, Two, and Three. Orbits could reveal launch sites, rocket strength, and the aims of each flight. The paper is mostly figures, the mathematics of the early space race set down for analysts. Pure data papers rarely survive in public files, and this one shows the raw layer beneath the polished estimates that reached presidents and shaped public claims.
cia-0000132302:
Iraqi ground forces are assessed in Situation Report 612 of the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 3, 1991. Saddam Hussein's army was often described in public debate as one of the largest in the world. Its troops were dug in across Kuwait and southern Iraq.

The report measures that ground threat as the agency itself judged it, apart from newspaper claims. Numbers, equipment, training, and readiness all mattered to planners weighing a land campaign. For readers, the entry shows the gap between the feared army of the headlines and the force analysts described. That judgment shaped choices made before the ground war began.
cia-0000132402:
Cuba is the subject of a CIA briefing given by the Director of Central Intelligence himself. The briefing is dated January 5, 1961. A new Kennedy administration was taking its first hard look at the Cuba problem that month.

When the director briefed in person, the subject sat at the top of the agency's list. The document preserves his assessment as he delivered it to senior officials. For readers, it marks the moment the incoming government inherited the Cuba file. Within months that file would produce the Bay of Pigs invasion and a lasting crisis with Havana.
cia-0000132502: Argentina sending special envoys to both the United States and Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1961. Buenos Aires was trying to place itself between Washington and Havana as a mediator. Mediating that quarrel would prove a thankless task for any government. The short document covers the planned mission and what Argentina hoped to gain from attempting it that winter.
cia-0000132602:
A large bloc arms shipment to Cuba fills item 16 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated August 5, 1960. Soviet weapons were now flowing to the island in real quantity, shipload after shipload.

The shipment marked a step up from the small buys of the spring. Two years later the same route would carry missiles. That cargo brought the world to the edge of nuclear war in the fall of 1962. For readers, the item is an early dated marker on that road. It shows the buildup while it could still be counted in loads of guns and shells rather than in rockets.
cia-0000135602: Spanish-language papers of the 2506 Brigade fill a CIA record carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. Three months stood between this record and the landing at the Bay of Pigs. The brigade's paperwork was piling up as training wound toward its end. The record stands beside an October 1960 file of the same kind. It keeps the Spanish text as filed.
cia-0000136302: Early decisive action is urged in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable, which lists the pressures closing in on the PBSUCCESS forces. Once the enemy doubts victory, it argues, he may demand quick enforcement of a UN cease-fire, while supply problems and reliance on air drops grow unsupportable. The cable calls for seizing ADAM, and possibly BOND as a base, with Plan Alpha's bombing of Matamoros as the softening-up step.
cia-0000137002: Act on embassy asylees now, this June 1954 cable suggests. It went to the Guatemala station chief. The junta should make its requests at the same time. All embassies harboring asylees should get one. The requests should rest on the danger the asylees pose. Demands should stay narrow. They should cover only hard-core communists and sympathizers. Criminal charges must be legally clear against them. Such charges should be drawn up quickly. The top cases need a legal basis first.
cia-0000140402: The hypnotic messenger is explained in this 1954 paper. It covers the military application of hypnotism. A subject can be sent to Berlin on a routine assignment. He carries a message he cannot betray. He will have no waking memory of its contents. He will have no knowledge of ever being hypnotized. Only Colonel X in Berlin can recover the message. His first advantage over an ordinary courier is clear. He can never slip and divulge a mission he does not consciously know.
un-sc-res-102:
Resolution 102 sets the terms for Japan to join the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Council adopted it on 3 December 1953. The vote was ten to none. The Soviet Union abstained. Japan was not yet a UN member. So the Charter required the General Assembly to fix the terms. It would act on advice from the Council.

Japan would join once it filed a signed statement with the Secretary-General. The statement also had to be ratified under Japanese law. In it, Japan would accept the Statute in full. It would accept the duties in Article 94 of the Charter. It would also agree to pay a fair share of the Court's costs. The Assembly would set that share after talks with Japan.
un-sc-res-302: The library catalogues Resolution 302, a Security Council decision, under the year 1971. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-402: Preserved as Resolution 402, this Security Council text carries a 1981 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1302: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 1302, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-2202:
Resolution 2202 gave the Security Council's backing to the Minsk agreements, the ceasefire deals meant to end fighting in eastern Ukraine. Rebels backed by Russia held parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The Council adopted the text days after the second Minsk deal was signed.

Inside, the members endorse the full package: a ceasefire, withdrawal of heavy weapons, local elections, and changes to Ukraine's constitution. They call on all sides to carry out every step. The resolution matters because it put the world's top security body behind a peace plan that both Ukraine and Russia had accepted.
cia-0000135702: One of the Spanish-language papers of Brigade 2506 bears the date 4 January 1961. plos-pone-0000002:
David Dingli and Jorge Pacheco tackled a size puzzle in blood biology in 2006. Hematopoietic stem cells, found in bone marrow, rebuild the blood and immune system for life. Only part of that pool works at any given time. The authors asked how the size of the active pool scales across mammals of very different body sizes.

Using allometric scaling, the math of how body features grow with size, they compared the active stem cell pool from small mammals to large ones. A clear scaling pattern would hint at shared rules governing blood production across species. Such rules help doctors think about marrow transplants and about why blood diseases strike as they do.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d102: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 8, 1943, in one of the last letters sent before his journey. It is Document 102 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Twenty days later the two men would shake hands at Tehran, ending two years of writing to a stranger. The record names the date and the leaders only. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series, at the edge of the voyage papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d202:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 9 November 1943, in telegram 1180, marked secret and personal. Roosevelt had handed him Harriman's message 6100, sent by Navy channels three days earlier, about the Allied agreement on Turkey.

Stettinius gives the answer Harriman needed. He is authorized to grant Molotov's request that his letter carrying the President's message on Turkey be made part of the secret military record of the Moscow conference. The short cable is the final Washington approval in that small chain of messages, which had begun with Harriman's own request from Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d302:
Civil affairs in France are the subject of a long secret telegram Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt from Washington on 24 November 1943. A paper on the subject, approved by Roosevelt, the War Department, and the British, had been sent to the Moscow conference and referred to the European Commission.

London now proposes a different approach. The French resistance is strongly represented on the French Committee at Algiers. Britain therefore argues that French cooperation in planning civil rule for liberated France can be won only one way. The matter must first be cleared with the Committee at government level. The British also expect the Soviets to raise the Committee's status at Tehran, and want an Anglo-American line agreed before that happens. A planners' note sketches a French director of civil affairs under the Allied commander.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d402:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote President Roosevelt a short personal letter at Tehran on 1 December 1943, his sixty-ninth birthday weekend, thanking him for a present. The gift, sent with a signed message of affection, was a beautiful bowl.

Churchill says he was indeed touched by the present. He will always treasure the bowl as a reminder of their sunlit days in Tehran. It also recalls the most memorable of his birthdays. He cannot thank Roosevelt enough, he adds, for all his friendship and support in the years they have worked together. He is glad of the occasion to send a message of sincere affection and gratitude. The letter is signed, as his letters to Roosevelt often were, yours always, Winston S. Churchill.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d502:
Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador to Turkey, was temporarily at Cairo when he wrote to Harry Hopkins on December 6, 1943. Turkey was the Second Cairo Conference's special business: Roosevelt and Churchill had just met President İnönü to urge Turkey toward the war. The State Department printed Steinhardt's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt, posted in Ankara, was Washington's expert on the Turkish question, and Hopkins was the man to reach at the President's side. Their exchange ties the embassy in Turkey directly to the summit's central negotiation. For readers, it shows specialized knowledge moving from the man on the spot to the center of power in a single step.
frus-1944-quebec-d102:
Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on August 30, 1944. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the final run of papers before the conference. Hull advised the President on all foreign affairs.

End-of-August letters from Hull carried the department's settled views. Roosevelt would host Churchill at Quebec within two weeks. Germany's future dominated the coming talks between them. Aid to Britain and the Pacific war also awaited decisions. For readers, the letter shows the Secretary of State briefing his President. He wrote in the last stretch of summit preparation.
frus-1944-quebec-d202:
At tea on September 15, 1944, Roosevelt received Empress Zita of Austria and her sons, the Archdukes Otto and Felix. No American record of the talk was found. The editors print a State Department translation of Otto's own memorandum, which reports the president's remarks on Austria, Hungary, and Russia in unusual detail.

Austria and Hungary, Roosevelt said, would undergo the least territorial change of any countries; only Transylvania was unclear. The main concern was keeping the Communists out of both, especially Hungary. If Hungary surrendered unconditionally to the Americans and British alone, she could be saved from communism and expect mild terms. Roosevelt liked Stalin personally, Otto recorded, but called him untrustworthy and deceitful.
frus-1944-quebec-d302: Editors of the Foreign Relations series supplied this short note, dated 19 September 1944, as document 302 of the Quebec volume. Editorial notes in the series explain gaps, point readers to related papers, or record facts the documents themselves leave unclear. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d102:
Archibald MacLeish wrote to Under Secretary Grew on 24 January 1945 with a reminder and a warning. MacLeish, an assistant secretary of state, asks Grew to raise one topic with the Secretary the next day. His top secret note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The topic is provisional governments in freed areas, Yugoslavia being the case in point. MacLeish wants the coming talks to seek a public pledge: such governments rest on the promise of free elections once elections are possible. Recognition should depend on those elections truly being held. Without such safeguards, he warns, the recent wave of disillusion will grow, and talk of Atlantic Charter principles will ring hollow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d202:
Admiral Leahy passed a draft message up to the President on 5 December 1944. His short note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, carries a text Stettinius suggested sending to Churchill that day. It concerns Stalin's two messages about de Gaulle.

The draft tells the prime minister that the President has received Stalin's messages of 2 and 3 December about his talks with the French leader. Stalin, the draft notes, sent Churchill identical messages of his own. Before answering Stalin, Roosevelt would like to have Churchill's views. The editors record that the message was in fact sent, as number 667. It is a small gear in the three-cornered exchange that ran ahead of the Big Three meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d302:
Grew kept the traveling Secretary fed with world news in this roundup of 31 January 1945. His top secret excerpts, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, gather the day's general information from Washington. Each item runs a line or two, and together they map the war's loose ends.

Winant is to act with his Soviet colleague in the European Advisory Commission to approve the French claims to equality on German matters. Under extreme Soviet pressure, the Czechoslovak cabinet has decided to recognize the Lublin Committee. Subasic waits in London until Tito recognizes the King's regency council. Greece is settling, with EAM accepting the government's plan for the peace talks. Bohlen, Grew adds, holds a long memorandum from Mikolajczyk proposing a settlement of the Soviet-Polish quarrel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d402:
Five Latin American states get a quiet push in Stettinius's cable to Grew of February 8, 1945. The five associated nations that had not yet declared war should be urged to do so at once. They should also adhere to the United Nations Declaration. The cable calls this absolutely essential by the end of the month.

Only if they acted in time would their step count for their interests — a seat at the founding conference. Knowledge of the message was limited to five named men in Washington. Stettinius signed off relying on Grew to renew the Department's recommendations. The wire shows the guest list being filled by pressure, in secret.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d502:
Germany must pay in kind. The protocol on reparations, agreed by the three heads of government at the Crimea Conference, opens with that rule. Payment would go first to the countries that bore the main burden of the war, suffered the heaviest losses, and organised victory over the enemy.

Reparation in kind would be exacted in three forms. The first was removals within two years of Germany's surrender, drawn from German national wealth at home and abroad. Equipment, machine tools, ships, and rolling stock are all named. The protocol fixed the principle and the forms. The famous sum — twenty billion, half to Moscow — stayed in the discussion record, not in this signed text.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d102:
General Deane sounded hopeful in a second telegram to General Bradley on June 26, 1945. The message is document 102 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. He had taken up the signal crews, the Zehlendorf scouting, and the air route once more, this time with Lieutenant General Slavin, who stood in for Antonov.

Deane hopes the communications men will be allowed in at once, with official approval possibly coming by telephone that night. Slavin asked how many men the signal work needed. Rather than lose time cabling Frankfurt, Deane answered 90. He judged that to be enough until July 1, when the Americans could move freely into their Berlin sector. He also hopes for answers on the Zehlendorf survey and on switching the air route from Stendal to Halle.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d202:
Ambassador Winant reported Eden's approval of the American agenda in a telegram from London on July 8, 1945. The personal message to Secretary Byrnes is document 202 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Washington's topic list had been delivered to the Foreign Office the day before.

In a brief talk over his private wire, Eden volunteered that he was very much pleased with the agenda as forwarded. Eden was about to come to London to act as Prime Minister while Churchill vacationed in France before the conference. Winant planned to dine alone with him on Tuesday and send a fuller account of the British reaction afterward. No report of that dinner has been found, a note in the volume adds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d302:
Ambassador Harriman cabled from Moscow at midnight on June 30, 1945, about reshaping Hungary's Allied Control Commission for the armistice's second period. He deferred to General Key in Budapest on which points belonged in new statutes. Key, he said, sat closer to the problem than the Moscow embassy did.

Harriman reported no answer from Molotov to his June 1 letter urging real three-power authority. He doubted Moscow would accept any plan letting British or American members block commission acts. Pressing too hard now, he advised, might do more harm than good. His caution captures the weak hand Washington held in Hungary.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d402:
French aims on the Rhine are summarized in extracts from a briefing book paper on France dated June 23, 1945. Paris had put forward no concrete proposals, the summary says, but the views of French officials could be stated. France disclaimed any design to annex German territory outright.

Instead, France wanted the Rhineland and Westphalia, including the Ruhr, separated from Germany. The two would be kept apart from each other, under distinct regimes. Ruhr-Westphalia would sit under an international regime. The Rhineland, from the Swiss frontier to beyond Cologne, would sit under permanent French military and economic control. That area takes in the Saar and bridgeheads on the right bank. Luxembourg, Belgium, and the Netherlands might share in the control.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d502:
Delivery of the recognition texts in Moscow is reported in Harriman's cable of July 5, 1945. That evening he delivered to the Polish ambassador the texts of the President's message to Osóbka-Morawski and of the public statement on recognition of the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. The ambassador expressed his appreciation for being provided with the texts.

He stated that he would transmit them to his government immediately. The announcement of recognition, he added, would appear in the next morning's papers in Poland. Harriman notes that the British ambassador was also sending a communication to the Polish ambassador that same evening, keeping the two recognitions in step.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d602:
A planning date for the end of Japan's organized resistance is set in a U.S. Chiefs of Staff memo of July 7, 1945. It is document 602 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The date was meant for staff talks with the British at the conference.

The chiefs propose November 15, 1946, as the planning date. It would guide factory output and the assignment of manpower, and it could be adjusted as the war went on. They also ask that the phrase end of the war be avoided in this context. Some U.S. laws lapse at set times after the end of a war. Those laws, the chiefs note, should stay in force through the occupation of Japan. The Combined Chiefs took up the paper at Potsdam on July 19.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d702:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a courtesy call by Turkey's ambassador in a memo dated July 7, 1945. It is document 702 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Baydur came with his secretary, who served as interpreter.

After talk of the San Francisco Conference's success, Baydur passed on his foreign minister's regrets. An early sailing from Boston had kept the minister from a hoped-for stop in Washington. Grew replied that he fully understood the reasons. Baydur then turned to the Moscow talks of three weeks before. He restated Molotov's three stated demands on Turkey. They were a rectification of the Turkish-Soviet frontier, bases on the Dardanelles, and a two-sided revision of the Montreux Treaty. The memo shows Ankara working Washington directly as the summit neared.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d802:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d902:

One clause stayed disputed. It would have paid for approved imports before reparation deliveries, while leaving Germans enough to live on. The sub-committee could not agree on it. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1002:

The clause would have the Control Council take control and power of disposal over German-owned external assets abroad. It covers assets not already held by Allied nations that fought Germany. The pair also wanted the matter named in the conference communiqué. Soviet members showed little interest and reserved their stand pending study. The attached third report records plainly that no decision was reached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1102:
Another working paper from the American team at Potsdam carries the date 25 July 1945. Like the papers drafted around it, it was staff work, written behind closed doors. Its job was to give United States negotiators a clear, agreed stand to carry into the talks.

By the second week the summit had moved past opening speeches into close bargaining over details. Papers of this sort were drafted, revised, and sometimes dropped as the talks shifted. This one holds a snapshot of the American team's thinking on a single day. Read with its companion papers, it shows a large staff machine at work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1202:
London's team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the summit's third day. British papers at this stage set out what the government wanted from the peace. Each gave the Americans and Soviets a clear British stand to answer.

The government behind this paper was itself days from falling. Churchill's team wrote the stand; another team would have to defend or drop it. That odd fact hangs over the British papers of the first week. This proposal is the formal British bid from the opening round, kept in the American files for later readers to weigh.

arxiv-2606-05502: The Laughlin wave function describes electrons in the fractional quantum Hall effect, one of physics' strangest phases of matter. arxiv-2606-05602: When AI tutors a human, correcting the move helps once — fixing the misunderstanding helps forever. arxiv-2606-06202: Inducibility asks how often a small pattern can appear inside a large graph — and blowup graphs push that question to extremes. This paper gives exact extremal constructions for their inducibility. Exact constructions settle questions that were previously only bounded.

arxiv-2606-06902: Post-training LLMs for specific tasks usually means full fine-tuning. TALAN does it with task-aligned latent adaptation networks: targeted adaptation in latent space. Johann Arndt published True Christianity in the seventeenth century, in German as Vier Bücher vom wahren Christentum. His argument rebuked comfortable churchgoers: real Christianity is not attendance or correct doctrine alone. It is an inward transformation of the heart that changes how a person lives.

Arndt calls readers to repentance, prayer, humility, and daily practice of faith rather than mere profession. The book proved hugely popular, was carried by missionaries around the world, and shaped Protestant piety for generations. Its stern, searching tone still explains its influence: Arndt measured religion by fruit in ordinary conduct, not by labels.

Charles Squire retold the myths of the British Islands, drawing on medieval Irish and Welsh sources. Cuchulain's heroics, the voyage of Bran, Arthur's court, and the old gods behind the tales all appear. Squire aimed at the general reader rather than the Celtic scholar.

Working as a storyteller with a scholar's conscience, he separates story from history where the evidence allows and admits where it does not. Gods become kings in some tales, heroes shrink or grow across versions, and Squire tracks the changes. V1 evidence calls the result the best single doorway into Celtic mythology; readers get narrative first, with learning carried lightly.

Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 after his fall from Florentine politics cost him office, freedom, and nearly his health under torture.
