His note to Clay kept the one friendly great court close, without taking its favor for granted. Favor not taken for granted stayed favor, a lesson Seward taught by letter after letter. Favor kept by care is the theme the Russian file sounds from start to end.
frus-1861-d302:
A letter home from Mr. Thayer, dated 20 July 1861, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 302 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d102:
In a report dated 17 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 102 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d202:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1862, in a letter printed as Document 202 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons had represented Britain in Washington since 1859 and knew the capital well.

A minister's letters to a secretary of state carried his government's questions, protests, and replies in formal form. Lyons used the channel briskly in early January as the Trent settlement closed. His note belongs to the file that documents how the two governments, having nearly fought, settled back into wary daily dealings. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d302:
On 9 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 302 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Seward wrote the day Cedar Mountain was fought in Virginia, though the result was not yet clear in Washington. His Paris letters that month worked to offset the gloom of a bad summer. For Dayton, each dispatch was both instruction and ammunition. Words he could use with French officials who read Union defeats as reasons to favor the South. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d402:
Horace J. Perry in Madrid received this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 May 1862. It appears as Document 402 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Late May 1862 found Union forces before Corinth and Richmond, and foreign courts watched to see if the rebellion would crack. Spain's court, ruling Cuba across a narrow sea from Florida, heard Confederate pleas often. An instruction like this one armed Perry with Washington's view of the war and its aims. The case for the Union was thus put in Madrid in Seward's own chosen words.
frus-1862-d502:
James Shepherd Pike received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1862. It is Document 502 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record.

Late May 1862 was a confident moment in Washington, with Richmond threatened and Corinth about to fall. Seward's orders abroad struck a firm note on neutral duties and on the hopeless state of the rebellion, as he saw it. Pike at The Hague was to carry that note to the Dutch government in his plain style. The dispatch belongs to the spring sequence in which the Union, for a few weeks, argued from strength in every capital in Europe.
frus-1862-d602:
Headed Despatch 10 and dated 15 April 1862, this paper concerns the extraordinary diplomatic mission of Spain in Mexico. It is Document 602 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the translated Spanish papers.

Mid-April 1862 was the hinge of the Mexican affair: the allies quarreled openly, and Spain and Britain moved to withdraw while France advanced alone. A Spanish paper of that date, numbered in its own series, belongs to the diplomacy of that breakup. The State Department printed such documents because the United States, absorbed in civil war, was managing Mexico by record and protest. The despatch is evidence in that record, in Spain's own hand.
frus-1862-d702:
Charles N. Riotte, the American minister in Costa Rica, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 May 1862. Riotte was a German-born lawyer whom Lincoln had sent to Central America. The letter is document 702 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Central America drew Washington's eye because any canal or transit route across the isthmus would run through it. Riotte's reports covered the small republics' politics and the safety of American trade and travel there. This dispatch is part of that watch. It is the ground-level record of a post that rarely made the news but sat on a route the whole world wanted.
frus-1863p1-d102:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863, the sixth of twelve dated that day in the file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 102 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Halfway through the batch, the shape of the day is clear: Seward worked down the London file point by point, one sheet each. The claims at stake were the war's claims — fair dealing, no aid to the South, no warships from British yards. This letter is the sixth stroke of that work. It takes its meaning from its place in the row, a brief rebuilt in a day.
frus-1863p1-d202:
On 18 May 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 202 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d302:
Reporting on 1 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 302 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d402:
On 24 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 402 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d502:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 8 May 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d602:
From Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 4 August 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020002:
Xavier I. Ambroggio, Douglas C. Rees, and Raymond J. Deshaies wrote this short study for PLOS Biology in 2004. It looks at a zinc-holding site called the JAMM motif. That motif appears in parts of two large cell machines: the proteasome, which breaks down worn proteins, and the signalosome, which helps control that process.

The two machines use their JAMM sites to snip small tags off proteins, a step that times when proteins are destroyed. The authors set out the shared shape and chemistry of the site in both machines. Seeing the same tool in two places hints at a common origin. It also gives chemists a defined pocket to study, and perhaps one day to block with a drug.
plos-pbio-0020402:
Cynthia Schuck-Paim, Lorena Pompilio, and Alex Kacelnik tested animal choice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Starlings choosing between food options sometimes seem to break the rules of rational choice, picking an option they earlier passed over. The authors show the birds' body state explains the odd picks.

A hungry bird values a meal differently than a full one, so its choices shift with its state. What looks like irrationality is a fixed rule applied under changing need. That is a sharp lesson for behavioral science. Before calling any choice irrational, in animals or people, check the state of the chooser. The paper refines how experiments on choice must be designed and read.
plos-pone-0000102:
Fatema A. Legrand, Douglas F. Nixon, Christopher P. Loo, and their team studied infants exposed to HIV in PLOS ONE in 2006. Some babies born to HIV-positive mothers escape infection, yet their immune systems met the virus. The team looked for HIV-specific T cell responses in these exposed but uninfected infants.

Strong responses appeared once regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes, were removed from the samples. That means the babies' killer T cells had indeed learned the virus, but their activity was being held down. The result speaks to vaccine hopes. Protection may already be within reach of the infant immune system. The brakes would need easing safely, at the right moment.
plos-pone-0000202:
Christel M. M. Mols and Marcel E. Visser published this orchard ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Great tits are small songbirds that feed their chicks on caterpillars. Working in commercial apple orchards, the authors report that great tits reduce the caterpillar damage done to the crop.

Birds as pest control is an old idea; this paper measures it in working orchards. Less caterpillar damage means more sound fruit without extra spraying. The findings support keeping nesting birds around farmland, a rare case where wildlife conservation and growers' profits point the same way.
plos-pone-0000302:
Chung-Der Hsiao, May-Su You, Ying-Jey Guh, and colleagues published this zebrafish development paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ionocytes are skin cells that manage salt and acid balance in fish. The authors show that two genes, foxi3a and foxi3b, form a positive regulatory loop, each switching the other on. That loop is essential for specifying and differentiating zebrafish epidermal ionocytes.

A self-reinforcing loop locks a cell into its identity once the decision starts. The paper traces that loop in the fish's skin. Zebrafish ionocytes are a model for salt-handling cells in other animals, including the human kidney, so the circuit matters beyond fish.
plos-pone-0000402:
Thomas Elmqvist and colleagues studied the fate of tropical dry forest in Madagascar, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. These forests are rich in unique species but easier to clear than rainforest, and much of Madagascar's has been lost. The team mapped patterns of loss and regrowth and asked how social institutions shape them.

Forests do not fall only to chainsaws; they fall or recover under rules about land, farming, and local authority. By tying forest change to that social and institutional context, the study shows why conservation plans succeed in one place and fail in another. Madagascar's dry forests, and the people living beside them, are the test case.
plos-pone-0000502:
Irina Chis Ster and Neil M. Ferguson reconstructed the numbers behind Britain's 2001 foot and mouth epidemic, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The outbreak led to the slaughter of millions of animals and fierce debate over control policy. The team estimated the transmission parameters of the epidemic in Great Britain: how readily the virus spread between farms and over distance.

Firm parameters are the difference between a model that argues and a model that persuades. With them, officials can test culling and vaccination strategies before the next outbreak. The study revisited the epidemic with complete data, supplying reference values for one of the most studied animal disease events on record.
plos-pone-0000602:
Javier Buceta and colleagues modeled a boundary that patterns the fly wing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The DV boundary separates the dorsal and ventral halves of the developing Drosophila wing, and a gene regulatory network maintains it. The team analyzed the robustness and stability of that network.

Robustness asks whether the boundary still forms when conditions wobble, as they always do in real embryos. A network model that stays stable under noise matches biology's reliability; one that shatters does not. Such modeling tells experimentalists which parts of the network carry the load of keeping development on track.
plos-pone-0000702:
Christopher B. Kaelin, Gregory M. Cooper, Arend Sidow and colleagues compared DNA sequences around a hunger gene across mammals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene makes agouti-related protein, a neuropeptide that stimulates food intake. In the brain it is produced only in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, a control center for appetite. Its levels rise when the body is in negative energy balance, burning more than it takes in.

How that regulation works at the molecular level was the open question. Comparing sequences across species highlights the stretches evolution kept, which usually mark functional control elements. Those conserved pieces tell researchers where to look for the switches governing hunger.
plos-pone-0000802:
Jacob S. Brenner and Ricardo E. Dolmetsch separated two calcium signals in heart muscle cells, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pathological cardiac hypertrophy, the thickening of heart muscle in disease, raises the risk of heart failure and cardiovascular death. Calcium-regulated gene expression is essential for inducing hypertrophy. The puzzle is how heart cells distinguish calcium signals that command growth from those that command each heartbeat.

Their title reports that the channel protein TrpC3 regulates hypertrophy-associated gene expression without affecting myocyte beating or cell size. A channel handling only the growth message is an attractive drug target: block the harmful growth signal, and the heartbeat's calcium stays untouched.
plos-pone-0000902:
Shengliang Zhang, Junwen Wang and Hung Tseng studied a protein that switches on a subset of ribosomal RNA genes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, basonuclin, is found mainly in skin type cells and in egg and sperm forming cells. Ribosomal RNA genes make the core parts of ribosomes, the cell's protein building machines.

Earlier lab work showed basonuclin binds the start region of these genes at three strong sites. Using HaCaT skin cells, the team asked which gene copies it actually regulates in living cells. The answer helps explain how cells tune protein production to match growth. It also clarifies a specialist protein with a narrow but key job.
plos-pone-0001002:
Alan Dabney and John Storey improved a simple classifier for reading genomic data, in a 2007 PLOS ONE methods article. Nearest centroid classifiers assign a sample to the closest group average. They have proved handy with genomic data, where thousands of genes are measured at once and samples are few.

The hard step is feature selection, picking which genes count. The authors drive that choice by optimality, choosing features by a stated best criterion rather than habit. A simple classifier done well can beat a complex one done loosely. Their method is aimed at labs that need clear calls from wide, noisy data.
plos-pone-0001102:
Aurelie Le Mandat Schultz, Arnaud Bonnard, Frederick Barreau and colleagues measured immune sensors in a rat model of a newborn gut disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Necrotizing enterocolitis is a devastating illness of premature infants, where gut tissue dies. Its cause combines several risk factors acting together, in the same setting where innate immunity switches on.

The team measured expression of TLR-2, TLR-4 and NOD2, sensors that detect germs, plus an activated inflammation factor, in newborn rats modeling the disease. If those sensors are part of the trigger, they become targets for protection. Premature guts meet bacteria before they are ready.
plos-pone-0001202:
BCAS3 is a gene of unknown function sitting in a region of chromosome 17 that is often amplified in cancer. Kavitha Siva and colleagues studied where the gene is active in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cancer often involves progressive changes in genes that are important for normal development.

The authors found the human gene expressed in embryonic stem cells and in vascular precursors, the cells that build blood vessels. That pattern suggests a role in human embryogenesis and in tumor angiogenesis, the growth of vessels that feed tumors. A development gene switched on in cancers is a lead worth following.
plos-pone-0001302:
Bark beetles find their host trees by smell, following pheromones and tree odors. Min Lu, Daniel Miller, and Jiang-Hua Sun report an interaction between two pine bark beetles in China. One is exotic and one is native. Their account appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Invasive species fascinate ecologists because they offer unique chances to study community ecology.

The authors describe cross-attraction between the two beetles and ask whether it is a novel invasion mechanism. If a native species' signals draw in an invader, or the reverse, the pair could reinforce each other's attacks on pines. Their study tests that possibility in the field.
plos-pone-0001402:
Miguel Bento and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on genome stress in a crop hybrid called triticale. When two species cross and the DNA doubles, the new genome faces a shock. Genes can be lost, moved, or switched off. The team asked whether this doubling acts as a force that pulls genomes back in size.

They tracked DNA shifts in triticale lines after the cross. Rearranged and lost stretches showed up in the new plants. The results back the idea that doubling can trim as well as add. That helps explain why plant genomes do not just grow without end after each round of doubling.
plos-pone-0001502:
Tige Rustad and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the TB germ answers low oxygen. Low oxygen zones in the body had long been tied to the latent, quiet phase of TB. Past work mapped the germ's first reply to low oxygen. The team tracked the longer, lasting reply that follows.

Their data show the germ settles into a steady state tuned to low oxygen. That state may be what lets TB hide for years in a host. Drugs that work on active germs may miss this quiet state. Naming its genes gives drug teams targets for the latent phase.
plos-pone-0001602:
Huan Chen and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a peroxide sensor in a hardy germ. Most germs sense peroxide, a toxic byproduct, with a protein that uses two sulfur atoms as the switch. The germ studied here shrugs off radiation and dryness that kill most kin. Its sensor was found to bear just one such sulfur atom.

Despite the lean build, the sensor still spots peroxide and switches on defense genes. A one atom switch breaks the standard design for this sensor family. The finding may help explain the germ's famed grit. It widens the known range of how cells sense harm.
plos-pone-0001702:
Simone Rossi, Alberto De Capua, Patrizio Pasqualetti, and their co-authors tested whether smells can move the motor system in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Watching actions or hearing action sounds is known to activate the viewer's own motor system across senses. Smell is the oldest sense, and it can steer behavior, yet its link to movement was untested.

Using transcranial magnetic stimulation, which probes motor excitability through the skull, the team measured cross-modal effects of odors on the motor system. They report distinct olfactory effects, per the paper's title. The full text gives the odors used, the stimulation results, and how effects differed by smell type. Results like these widen the picture of how the senses jointly prepare the body to act.
plos-pone-0001802:
Heather Powell, Joanne Smart, Lisa G. Wood, and their co-authors tested a symptom questionnaire in asthma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The Common Cold Questionnaire, or CCQ, is used to tell who has a viral infection and who does not. Its usefulness in people with acute asthma was unknown, though colds are a top trigger of asthma attacks.

The team assessed whether the CCQ can detect viral infection and monitor recovery during virus-induced asthma exacerbations. The full text gives the patient results, the virus tests, and how well questionnaire scores matched them. A cheap questionnaire that reliably flags viral attacks could steer asthma care and research without waiting for lab results.
plos-pone-0001902:
Sampson Kyere and co-authors probed the shape of a small viral protein part in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The part, called p12, sits inside the Gag building blocks of a mouse leukemia virus. It plays key roles as the virus is built, copies its genes, and slips its DNA into the host cell.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, a method that maps atomic shape, the team studied p12 joined to its next-door part in Gag. They report that p12 has no fixed fold in that construct; it stays loose and unstructured. A loose part can still be vital, since loose regions often serve as flexible links or binding pads.
plos-pone-0002002:
Zilal Kattan and co-authors studied a DNA repair protein that also shapes breast cancer growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, DDB2, helps fix DNA damage by nucleotide excision repair. It also plays roles in normal cells, such as gene control and cell cycle timing. Loss of DDB2 had been tied to a higher risk of tumors.

The team tested what DDB2 does inside breast cancer cells as they grow. If a repair protein also brakes or spurs growth, its loss could drive cancer by two paths at once. Work of this kind refines which tumors might react to drugs that target DNA repair.
plos-pone-0002102:
Thomas Jensen and co-authors split the roles of two forms of an energy enzyme in mouse muscle, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The enzyme, AMPK, is a promising drug target for metabolic disorders, in part because it promotes glucose uptake in skeletal muscle without insulin. It comes in two catalytic forms, alpha one and alpha two, and the alpha two form was clearly required for some uptakes.

As the title states, alpha one activation is required for glucose uptake driven by twitch contraction, but not for uptake driven by hydrogen peroxide. Two forms, two triggers: the split refines which form a drug should hit.
plos-pone-0002202:
Puspha Sinnayah, Erin Jobst, Joseph Rathner, and co-authors asked how cannabis-like drugs drive hunger, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cannabinoids, the active parts of marijuana, stir appetite, while drugs that block their main receptor, CB1, suppress appetite and aid weight loss. How these effects run through the brain's feeding circuits was unclear.

The team tested whether the melanocortin system, a known appetite control circuit, carries the feeding effect. They report that cannabinoid-driven feeding works independently of that system. The result redraws part of the hunger map and hints that appetite drugs may need to aim at more than one circuit at once.
plos-pone-0002302:
Shanthi Muttukrishna, Sangeeta Suri, Nigel Groome, and co-authors measured growth factors and oxygen inside the early pregnancy sac, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In the first trimester, a steep oxygen gradient runs between the mother's circulation and the tissues of the gestational sac. That gradient helps steer how the placenta's trophoblast cells behave.

The team asked whether the oxygen level inside the sac shapes the making of TGF beta proteins, signals that control cell growth. They measured both in early human pregnancies. Knowing how oxygen tunes placental signals bears on healthy placenta growth and on problems like miscarriage and pre-eclampsia that begin in these weeks.
plos-pone-0002402:
Work from Burgevin and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Anne Burgevin, Loredana Saveanu, Yohan Kim, and others. Its subject is a Detailed Analysis of the Murine TAP Transporter Substrate Specificity. The transporter linked to antigen processing (TAP) supplies cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for binding to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules.

Its specificity therefore influences the repertoire of peptides presented by MHC molecules. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002502:
In 2008, Loarie and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Scott R. Loarie, Benjamin E. Carter, Katharine Hayhoe, and others. Its subject is climate Change and the Future of California's Endemic Flora. The flora of California, a global biodiversity hotspot, includes 2387 endemic plant taxa.

With anticipated climate change, we project that up to 66% will experience >80% reductions in range size within a century. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002602:
A research team led by Saayman reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sheena Saayman, Samantha Barichievy, Alexio Capovilla, and others. Its subject is the Efficacy of Generating Three Independent Anti-HIV-1 siRNAs from a Single U6 RNA Pol III-Expressed Long Hairpin RNA. RNA Interference (RNAi) effectors have been used to inhibit rogue RNAs in mammalian cells.

However, rapidly evolving sequences such as the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) require multiple targeting approaches to prevent the emergence of escape variants. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002702:
Hoang Hoa Long led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was native bacterial endophytes promote host growth in a Species-Specific manner; phytohormone manipulations do not result in common growth responses. Authorship is credited in the record to Hoang Hoa Long and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. All plants in nature harbor a diverse community of endophytic bacteria which can positively affect host plant growth. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002802:
Aron J. Fazekas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was multiple multilocus DNA barcodes from the plastid genome discriminate plant species equally well. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Aron J. Fazekas, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. A universal barcode system for land plants would be a valuable resource, with potential utility in fields as diverse as ecology, floristics. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002902:
Perayot Pamonsinlapatham, Réda Hadj-Slimane, Françoise Raynaud and co-authors built a peptide tool against Ras signaling in 2008. RasGAP normally switches Ras off, but it also helps Ras and can block cell death through its SH3 domain. That second role does not depend on its switching job.

The team used a peptide aptamer, a short crafted protein piece, aimed at the RasGAP SH3 domain. In PLOS ONE they report it blocked a RasGAP link to Aurora and drove tumor cell death without using caspases, the usual death enzymes. Cancer researchers get a fresh angle on a well-known pathway.
plos-pone-0003002:
Jung Kyoon Choi, Sohyun Hwang and Young-Joon Kim studied chromatin silencing and stress response in yeast in 2008. Cells balance variety against fidelity by controlling random molecular noise. Epigenetic silencing, switching genes off via chromatin state, plays a critical role when environments change.

The team shows incomplete silencing increases random noise in gene expression in yeast. That noise can be a feature, letting a uniform population hedge bets under stress. Published in PLOS ONE, the study frames silencing as both a stabilizer and a source of useful diversity in genomic responses. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003102:
Krishnaraj Rajalingam, Manu Sharma, Christine Lohmann and co-authors studied apoptosis resistance in Chlamydia-infected cells in 2008. Chlamydia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause a variety of human diseases. Infected cells are protected against many different triggers of apoptosis, planned cell death.

That resistance is thought to be an important immune escape mechanism letting the bacteria persist. Mcl-1 is a key regulator of that resistance, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, blocking Mcl-1 might let infected cells die on schedule, a possible treatment angle. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003202:
Olyana N. Grod, Amber E. Budden, Tom Tregenza and colleagues survey peer reviewers in ecology and evolution in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Referee traits and their effects on peer review matter because the integrity of the system depends on fair evaluation of merit. In 2006 the team conducted an online survey of 1,334 ecologists and evolutionary biologists.

They report systematic variation in reviewer practice according to country and gender. Readers get data on a process usually hidden behind closed editorial doors. Evidence on reviewer differences can inform fairer review policies, even if it cannot settle every bias claim.
plos-pone-0003302:
Samuel Huber, Jörg Schrader, Gerhard Fritz and colleagues study a kinase needed for regulatory T cell conversion in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells are important mediators of immune tolerance. A subset can be generated in the periphery by TGF-beta dependent conversion of conventional CD4+CD25- T cells into induced regulatory T cells. In chronic viral infection or malignancy, such induced cells matter greatly.

The title reports that p38 MAP kinase signaling is required for conversion into induced Treg. Readers learn of a specific signaling step behind tolerance formation. Blocking or boosting that step could shift immune balance in autoimmunity or cancer.
plos-pone-0007402:
Nicola Canessa, Matteo Motterlini, Cinzia Di Dio, and colleagues scanned brains while people judged others' regret in 2009. Earlier studies showed understanding others' basic emotions uses a resonant mechanism. The observer's brain reactivates areas linked to those same experiences, allowing shared feeling without direct experience of the event itself.

The authors ask whether that mechanism extends to regret, a complex social emotion. They use functional MRI during regret judgments. Their PLOS ONE study investigates how the brain understands regret felt by another person. The answer informs theories of empathy, which matter for social behavior and its disorders.
plos-pone-0007502:
Vijaya Ramachandran and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on pancreatic cancer and a growth signal called adrenomedullin. Pancreatic tumors produce large amounts of this signal. It stimulates the cancer cells, raising growth and spread. The team examined the receptor that receives the signal, ADMR. They looked at tumor cells and at the supporting cells around the tumor as well.

ADMR proved to mediate the signal's effects on both fronts. Cancer cells respond through it, and so do cells of the tumor's microenvironment. Blocking that one doorway could therefore starve the tumor's whole growth network. Pancreatic cancer badly needs new points of attack. A shared receptor on tumor and support tissue is an efficient one. The study gives drug developers a defined target to test.
plos-pone-0007602:
David Katz and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on involving men in HIV testing during pregnancy. When male partners join antenatal counseling and testing, uptake of steps that protect babies rises. Yet men rarely attend. Working in a resource-limited setting, the team asked men directly for their views. The goal was practical: find methods that would actually bring fathers in.

Men's answers pointed to concrete barriers and workable invitations. Clinics learned what times, messages, and formats men would accept. That kind of listening turns a known good idea into an achievable one. Mother-to-child transmission can be cut sharply when both parents engage. The study treats men as partners in prevention rather than as obstacles. Its lessons apply wherever antenatal programs struggle to reach fathers.
plos-pone-0007702:
Avelin Aghokeng and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines HIV testing in Cameroon, where wider access to treatment depends on correct diagnosis. The country carries both major forms of the virus, group M and group O.

The team checked the HIV tests and testing plans then in use. They found that some infections, in particular group O, were missed or misread. A wrong result can deny a patient treatment or give false reassurance. The authors argue that better test choices are key to fair access to HIV care in Cameroon.
plos-pone-0007802:
Rui-Wu Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the partnership between fig trees and fig wasps. Wasps pollinate the figs, but they also lay eggs in the flowers. Their larvae gall and eat some of the seeds.

The tree gains because wasp offspring carry its pollen away. It loses if wasps take too many seeds. The authors show that wasp competition and high temperatures curb wasp virulence. That restraint keeps the exchange from tipping over. The work explains how this famous mutualism stays stable over time.
plos-pone-0007902:
Maria Cerezo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It checks the stability of mitochondrial DNA in a slow-moving leukemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia builds up lymphocytes in blood, marrow and lymph tissue. Earlier findings suggested mitochondrial DNA might play an important role in the disease.

Mitochondrial DNA often mutates in other cancers, so change was expected. The team analyzed its control region in patients. Against expectation, they found high stability in this leukemia. A stable mitochondrial genome is itself a clue. It suggests this cancer's energy machinery follows different rules from many tumors.
plos-pone-0008002:
Rachana Agarwal and colleagues studied a cell glue protein lost in stomach cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, claudin-11, helps seal the tight joins between cells. Sealed joins keep tissue in order; loose joins let cells wander.

In gastric cancer cells, the gene for this protein was silenced, and the cells pushed into new territory more readily. Loss of glue thus doubles as loss of a leash. The finding suggests that restoring the protein, or the paths it guards, might restrain this cancer's spread. Such silencing is common in tumors that learn to break free of their tissue.
plos-pone-0008102:
Peter McCormick and colleagues traced a stuck-on immune receptor in a rare disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. WHIM syndrome leaves people prone to warts and infections. Its cause is a cut tail on the receptor CXCR4, which guides immune cells around the body.

A healthy receptor calls in two proteins that shut it off and pull it inside the cell. The cut receptor failed to call them, so it stayed loud on the surface. That stuck signal explains much of the cells' odd behavior in WHIM, and names the shutoff crew as a treatment clue.
plos-pone-0008202:
Simone Wüst and colleagues tested a new steroid-like drug in mice in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. The drug targets the glucocorticoid receptor, a switch for inflammation. Classic steroids help many disorders but cause harsh side effects. A dissociating ligand aims to keep the benefit while avoiding the harm. That split rests on two modes of receptor action.

The team challenged that hope in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. They measured both healing effects and adverse effects of the ligand. The results test whether benefit and harm can truly be separated. The answer matters for safer anti-inflammatory drugs.
plos-pone-0008302:
Uwe Jerke and colleagues studied a transcription factor in blood cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Stat proteins carry signals from outside the cell to its genes. They cross into the nucleus through the nuclear pore complex. That complex acts as a selective filter for protein import. When monocytes mature, Stat1 must reach the nucleus to work.

The team found the protein nucleolin helps move Stat1 into the nucleus. This translocation happened upon monocyte differentiation. A dedicated carrier for a key signal protein is notable. It adds detail to how immune cells switch on their mature programs.
plos-pone-0008402:
Natalia V. Strunnikova and colleagues studied an inherited eye disease in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Choroideremia is a progressive X-linked disorder that destroys the retina. Mutations in the CHM gene cause it, disabling a protein called REP-1. REP-1 escorts Rab proteins through a chemical step called prenylation. Without that step, certain Rabs are under-prenylated and transport inside cells falters.

The team studied fibroblasts and monocytes from choroideremia patients. Loss of REP-1 function affected intracellular transport in those cells. Tracing that defect explains how the mutation blinds patients. It may also reveal treatment points.
plos-pone-0008502:
Ozlem Equils and co-authors build a computer model of preterm labor in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Preterm labor threatens babies born too early. Enough lab and animal data now exist to model the womb muscle in labor. The muscle, called the myometrium, contracts to deliver a baby. The model lets the team test disease paths in silico, meaning in a computer.

They simulate treatment with progesterone, a hormone that can calm the womb. They also simulate a Cox2 inhibitor, a drug that blocks inflammation signals. The model predicts how each drug might delay labor. Such trials in a computer can guide real clinical studies.
plos-pone-0008602:
Norbert Babai and co-authors study calcium channels in lab cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. L-type calcium currents are influenced by chloride levels outside cells. But the sites where anions act had not been identified. The team express CaV1.2 channels in HEK293 cells. Those channels are the main L-type form in heart and brain. Replacing external chloride strongly inhibits the channel currents in their tests.

They map anion-sensitive regions of the CaV1.2 channel. Those regions explain how chloride tunes channel activity. Calcium channels control heartbeat, hormone release, and nerve signals. Knowing their anion sites may matter for drugs that target them.
plos-pone-0008702:
Eiron Cudaback, William Marrs, Thomas Moeller, and colleagues asked how receptor counts shape a drug effect. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used astrocytoma cells, a kind of brain tumor. Cannabis compounds can push such tumor cells to die. Two docking sites, CB1 and CB2, catch those compounds. Which site does the work was unsettled.

The researchers built tumor cell lines with set amounts of each receptor. They then dosed the cells and watched for self-destruction, called apoptosis. The balance of CB1 and CB2 decided how strong the killing was. Tumor tests may need receptor counts before cannabis-based treatment makes sense.
plos-pone-0008802:
Irene Lurkin, Robert Stoehr, Carolyn Hurst, and colleagues built a fast mutation test for cancer care. Their assay study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some advanced colorectal cancers resist drugs aimed at a growth receptor. Resistance follows mutations in genes like KRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA. Testing each mutation separately wastes tissue and time. Clinics needed one combined check.

Their two multiplex assays read twenty-two mutation sites at once. Four genes are covered in the same workflow. Validation showed the combined test catches the key changes reliably. Faster genotyping helps oncologists skip drugs that cannot work for a patient.
plos-pone-0008902:
Catherine Hyams, Jerry Tam, Jeremy Brown, and colleagues tested whether HIV weakens a germ-tagging defense. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia and meningitis, often in HIV patients. The complement system tags germs so immune cells can grab them. Tags called C3b and iC3b are central to that marking. The team suspected HIV patients might tag pneumococcus poorly, perhaps through low antibody levels.

Tagging on the germ proved just as strong in HIV-positive samples. The hypothesis failed its direct test. Pneumonia risk in HIV must come from other breaks in defense. A clean negative result redirects research to likelier causes.
plos-pone-0009002:
Anup Sharma and co-authors linked one altered protein to the clutter found in several brain diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's share some features despite their differences. Clumps called inclusions build up in nerve cells, synapses fail early, and certain neurons die. Few molecules had been tied to all of those shared features.

The team found a phosphorus-tagged form of the protein Elk-1 inside the inclusions. This form appears toxic and turns up across multiple neurodegenerative diseases. One molecule linking clumps and neuron loss gives researchers a common thread. Following it could reveal shared drug targets for diseases usually studied apart.
plos-pone-0009102:
Martijn Weisfelt and co-authors charted meningitis cases in patients with alcohol problems, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heavy drinking leaves people open to infections, above all pneumonia of the lungs. Meningitis, infection of the membranes around the brain and cord, is another threat. The cases studied were caught outside hospitals, in daily life.

The team set these patients' cases beside those of adults who did not drink heavily. Symptoms, germs, and outcomes differed between the two groups. The drinking group often arrived sicker and fared worse in the end. A clear chart of these patterns helps doctors spot the disease early in this group.
plos-pone-0009302:
Rex Jung and co-authors published this lupus brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that attacks many organs. Some patients develop central nervous system involvement, classed as neuropsychiatric lupus. That form can bring seizures, psychosis, and thinking problems, and it is hard to measure.

The team used brain imaging to compare patients with this neuropsychiatric form. They measured the thickness of the cortex and the volume of deep gray matter. Both were reduced in these patients. Objective brain measures like these could help doctors recognize and track a disease that otherwise hides behind varied symptoms.
plos-pone-0011402:
Keith Ballingall and co-authors studied immune genes in domestic sheep in 2010 and found a pattern that crosses species lines. The genes in question help the immune system display germ fragments to patrolling cells, and variety in them helps flocks survive new diseases. Some variants in sheep turned out to be older than sheep themselves as a species.

Those shared variants, kept across species by natural selection, are called trans-species polymorphism. Their survival implies the variants were so useful that evolution retained them while species split apart. For sheep breeding, the finding counsels care: breeding purely for production could discard ancient immune variety that flocks may need in a future outbreak. For evolution, it shows selection can preserve useful immune options far longer than a single species lasts.
plos-pone-0011502:
Corey Frucht and co-authors searched in 2010 for what switches on cell growth in the bird inner ear. Birds, unlike mammals, can regrow damaged hearing cells, and the basilar papilla is the tissue where that regrowth happens. The team treated the tissue with forskolin, a chemical that provokes growth, and read which genes and microRNAs changed as cells began to divide.

They identified microRNA-181a as a mediator of the growth response, a small RNA that helps carry the signal from treatment to division. Naming the middleman matters, because a defined molecule can be tested, blocked, and perhaps one day borrowed. Mammals cannot regrow hearing cells, and every step of the bird pathway that is mapped is a candidate step to restart in human ears. The study is basic science with a clear long-term hope behind it.
plos-pone-0011602:
Yasuhito Shirai and co-authors studied an enzyme that helps brain cells build connections, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, called DGK beta, is common in brain areas tied to thought and memory, including the cortex and hippocampus. It converts one fatty signal molecule into another, but its exact job in neurons was unclear.

The team showed that DGK beta is needed for neurons to grow spines, the tiny knobs where nerve cells receive signals. Without it, spine formation falters. Since spines underpin learning, the result links a single enzyme to the physical basis of mental function and suggests a new angle on disorders of thinking.
plos-pone-0011702:
Sarah To and co-authors studied layered controls on a family of gene switches, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CP2 family of transcription factors turns genes on across many tissues. One member, CRTR-1, is unusual because it appears only at specific places and times, and removing it disrupts the maturation of the organ it serves.

The team showed that CRTR-1 and a chemical tag called sumoylation both modulate the family's activity. Two different modifiers tuning the same switches gives cells finer control over gene programmes. Such layered management is likely a general feature of development, not a quirk of one family.
plos-pone-0011802:
Jennifer Hsu and co-authors studied meal-time excitement in mice that lack a serotonin receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Animals can tune their daily clocks to food times, growing active just before a meal is due. That meal-anticipation behaviour helps survival, but the molecules and brain paths behind it were not fully known.

Mice with no serotonin 2C receptor showed stronger meal anticipation, tied to more activity in brain paths outside the hypothalamus. The find shows the circuits of hunger reach far past the usual brain spots. It may also help explain appetite troubles tied to serotonin signals.
plos-pone-0011902:
Delira Robbins and co-workers studied in 2010 whether a plant-based supplement could help prevent skin cancer. The supplement, Protandim, blends five medicinal plants and is known to raise the body's own antioxidant enzymes. The team focused on events inside cells as skin tumors form, including the movement of the guardian protein p53 into mitochondria.

Tracking that movement and the resulting cell death offers a concrete check on claims of cancer prevention. Supplements are often sold on antioxidant language alone, so mechanistic evidence matters. If boosting internal defenses also pushes damaged skin cells to die on cue, that is a stronger and more testable basis for prevention than marketing suggests.
plos-pone-0012002:
You Jin Hong, Paul Marjoram, and Darryl Shibata proposed in 2010 reading a tumor's family history from chemical marks on its DNA. Watching a human tumor grow over time is impractical, so its history must be inferred from the variation among its cells today. The more differences on average, the longer the tumor has been growing and branching.

Methylation patterns, chemical tags that shift as cells divide, serve as the record they used to infer tumor ancestry. Reconstructing that ancestry shows whether a cancer spread early or late and how its parts relate. Such histories could eventually help judge which parts of a tumor carry the dangerous lineages.
plos-pone-0012102:
Wieke Altorf-van der Kuil, Mariëlle Engberink, Elizabeth Brink, and colleagues reviewed the research on protein in the diet and blood pressure for PLOS ONE in 2010. High blood pressure is common worldwide and is a major cause of heart disease and stroke. Diet is one of the few levers people can adjust daily, and protein intake had drawn growing interest as a possible part of that lever.

A review pulls all the published studies together and weighs them as a whole, instead of trusting any single trial. The authors gathered that full record on dietary protein and blood pressure. Reviews of this kind shape the advice doctors and health agencies give, because they show where the evidence is firm and where it is still thin.
plos-pone-0012202:
Tai-Ho Hung, Szu-Fu Chen, Meng-Jen Li, and co-authors tested vitamin C and E on placenta cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Giving both vitamins in pregnancy had been linked to harm in some trials. The women in those trials faced a dangerous blood pressure condition. Harms included low birth weight and early birth, and no one knew why. The placenta's surface cells face cycles of low and returning oxygen. Those cycles look much like the ones in that condition.

Under those oxygen swings, the vitamins changed cell death and self-recycling. The effects differed from those under steady oxygen. In short, context flips the vitamins from help to harm. The work warns against trusting supplements in pregnancy just because they are familiar. It also points at the mechanism behind the reported harms.
plos-pone-0012302:
Alexander Lorestani, Lilach Sheiner, Kevin Yang, and co-authors disabled a division protein in the Toxoplasma parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, MORN1, is kept across the whole parasite group that includes malaria, and it sits in several structures tied to cell division. Toxoplasma divides by an internal budding process simpler than most, making it a good place to dissect the protein's job.

Without MORN1, the parasites kept starting divisions they could not finish properly: the base of the new cells assembled badly, the internal organelle failed to split, and final separation failed. A protein this central to division in a group of major parasites is a plausible drug target, provided human cells lack its twin role.
plos-pone-0012402:
Michelle Hildebrandt, Ritsuko Komaki, Zhongxing Liao and colleagues hunted gene clues to radiation harm in lung cancer care, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Radiation and chemo-radiation cure some non-small cell lung cancers, but they often inflame the food pipe and lungs. Doctors cannot yet tell in advance which patients will suffer the worst side effects.

The team linked variants in inflammation genes to higher risk of esophagitis and pneumonitis after treatment. If confirmed, a gene test before therapy could flag fragile patients for gentler plans or closer watching. It is a step toward cancer care fitted to the patient, not just to the tumor.
plos-pone-0012502:
Ifedayo Adetifa, Martin Ota, Brigitte Walther and colleagues tracked a TB blood test during treatment, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of newly diagnosed patients. The test, an interferon gamma release assay, measures immune memory of TB germs. If its signal fades predictably as drugs work, clinics could use it to monitor therapy and compare new regimens.

The team measured how fast the signal decayed once anti-tuberculosis therapy began. The decay pattern was slower and messier than a simple cure meter would need. Their caution saves programs from over-trusting one number and points to what a true treatment-monitoring biomarker must still prove.
plos-pone-0012602:
Das, Ghosh, Manna and co-authors tested whether taurine can shield the liver from arsenic harm. Arsenic poisons the liver in part by draining glutathione, a key defence against chemical stress. Taurine, a compound found in many tissues, helps cells make more glutathione, but its exact protective route was unclear.

Their 2010 rat and cell work traces taurine's effect through a chain involving the proteins PKC delta and JNK. Blocking that chain kept liver cells from dying by the self-destruct route called apoptosis. The findings matter where arsenic in water remains a daily health threat.
plos-pone-0012702:
Hatakeyama, Cheng, Wirth and co-authors traced how head and neck cancers escape a targeted drug. Cetuximab blocks the EGFR growth receptor, yet tumours often learn to resist it over time. Their 2010 study proposed that long blockade makes the cancer raise levels of the receptor's own trigger molecules.

One such trigger, HB-EGF, turned out to be raised by a small RNA called miR-212 falling away. Restoring that balance could revive the drug's power. The chain they outline gives doctors a marker for resistance and a possible way around it.
pmc-10200802:
Chen, Saeed, Liu and co-authors reviewed the roles of macrophages in controlling immunity and in treatment, in a 2023 article. Macrophages live in most tissues, body cavities and mucosal surfaces. They form a core part of the innate immune system, eating germs and shaping later immune responses.

The review gathers what is known about how these cells switch between attack and repair states, and how that switching affects disease. It also surveys treatments that aim to steer macrophages in cancer, infection and chronic inflammation. Such steering is a growing drug strategy.
pmc-1239902:
Sporns, Tononi, and Kotter propose mapping the human connectome, the full network of links inside the human brain. They argue that such a connection map would form an essential base for both basic and applied brain research. At the time they wrote, that wiring was still largely unknown.

Their paper lays out a structural picture: which brain parts connect to which, and how that web could be charted. Knowing the wiring should help explain how the brain works as a system, not just as separate regions. The connectome idea went on to shape large mapping projects worldwide.
pmc-1852402:
Hellemans, Mortier, De Paepe, and co-authors present qBase, a free program for handling real-time PCR data. PCR tests that track DNA growth are used to measure gene activity. Raw output from many samples and genes is hard to manage and easy to mishandle by hand.

qBase organises that data and automates the relative quantification step, which compares gene activity between samples. Automated, standard handling cuts errors and makes results easier to repeat. For labs running gene tests daily, shared software of this kind raised the reliability of reported changes in gene activity.
pmc-3412702:
Ye, Coulouris, Zaretskaya, and co-authors present Primer-BLAST, a tool to design target-specific primers for PCR. Primers are the short DNA pieces that start copying in a PCR test. Choosing them well is probably the single most important factor in whether the reaction works.

Specific copying requires primers that do not match other targets in the wrong orientation or at the wrong distance. Primer-BLAST checks candidate primers against sequence databases for such stray matches. The free tool saves labs from failed reactions and false results, and it is built into routine test design.
pmc-3965102:
Law, Knox, Djoumbou, and their team presented DrugBank version four in 2013. DrugBank is a free online database that holds deep detail on drugs, how they act, and what they target in the body. First described in 2006, it had grown fast as users asked for more.

The new release put fresh weight on drug metabolism, the way the body changes and clears a drug. Entries link a drug to its targets, enzymes, and chemical facts in one place. Doctors, chemists, and drug makers use that joined-up view to check safety, plan trials, and hunt for new uses of known drugs.
pmc-4029002:
Rosano and Ceccarelli reviewed in 2014 how to make proteins in the bacterium Escherichia coli. This microbe is one of the top choices for producing recombinant proteins, meaning proteins from genes placed into it on purpose. Its use as a living factory is well established and very common.

The review covers the many tools and protocols built for high-level production in this host. It also faces the hard parts, such as proteins that fold badly or form clumps. Clear guidance on strain choice, gene design, and growth conditions helps labs raise yields. Such proteins are used in research, medicine, and industry.
pmc-4383202:
Wan, Wang, Liu, and their co-authors tackled a common problem in meta-analysis in 2014. Reviews often need to pool the mean and standard deviation from similar clinical trials. Many trials, though, report only the median, the range, or the quartiles instead.

The authors give formulas to estimate the mean and spread from those reported values. Their methods were tested and compared so users can pick the best fit for each case. Without such estimates, many trials would be dropped from a review, wasting their evidence. The paper is a practical aid used by review teams across medicine.
pmc-4748402:
Atanasov, Waltenberger, Pferschy-Wenzig, and their colleagues reviewed plant-derived natural products in 2015. Medicinal plants have a long record as sources of molecules with therapeutic value. They still form an important pool for finding new drug leads today.

For some decades, industry focused mainly on libraries of synthetic compounds instead. The review covers both discovery of active plant products and the resupply problem, since a rare plant may not yield enough material. Solving supply through farming or synthesis decides whether a lead becomes a drug. The paper supports renewed investment in plant sources for future medicines.
pmc-5641502:
The GBD 2015 Neurological Disorders Collaborator Group published this large study in 2017. It measures how much illness, disability, and early death brain and nerve disorders caused around the world. The work covers global, regional, and national levels for the years from 1990 to 2015.

Readers get comparable figures for conditions such as stroke, dementia, epilepsy, and Parkinson disease across many countries and years. Health planners need numbers like these to decide where staff, beds, and money should go. The study shows that the share of disease linked to nerve disorders grew as populations aged, which makes planning harder.
pmc-6602502:
Stephan Greiner, Pascal Lehwark, and Ralph Bock presented OGDRAW version 1.3.1 in 2019. Chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes are small circles packed with genes. Drawing clear maps of them is a routine need as sequencing floods in.

OGDRAW turns genome annotation into publication-ready circular maps automatically. The update expands the toolkit and eases work on many genomes at once. Users can tune colors and layout without drawing by hand. Plant and organelle researchers use the maps in papers and teaching to show gene order at a glance. Maps can be exported in formats ready for journals, posters, and genome database pages.
pmc-6678302:
Laura Doyle and Matthew Wang gave an overview of extracellular vesicles in 2019. Cells release tiny vesicles, including exosomes, that carry markers of their state. Those parcels show up in blood and other fluids, which makes them tempting for tests.

Clinical use is held back by a lack of standard ways to isolate and measure vesicles. The authors review origins, contents, and the main separation methods, with the strengths of each. They stress reporting standards so studies can be compared. The overview helps newcomers avoid the field's common traps. Practical tables compare yield, purity, and cost across the main isolation methods.
plos-pone-0360002:
Zuzanna Gurzyńska and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines academic stress among students. The authors focus on two resources students draw on: coping strategies, the ways they handle pressure, and psychological resilience, the capacity to recover from setbacks.

The study asks how these two resources shape the level of stress students report. If certain coping styles clearly soften stress, universities can teach them rather than only treating stress after it harms grades or health. Counselors and student support services are the readers who would turn such findings into workshops and advising.
plos-pone-0349302:
Muhammad Awais and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It reports new inhibitors of fucosyltransferase-8, an enzyme that attaches a sugar called fucose to proteins. The approach integrates three kinds of evidence: biochemical, biophysical, and computer-based.

This enzyme's sugar-tagging is linked to cancer spread and other diseases, so blockers are sought as drug leads. Combining three method families makes a candidate far sounder than any single test alone. Medicinal chemists and researchers who study sugar chains on proteins are the readers for new inhibitor candidates.
plos-pone-0350902: Tozzo and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on people with long-term shoulder pain. While volunteers simply watched pictures of shoulder movements, the team tracked changes in heart rhythm and how sensitive each person was to pain. The heart signal shows how the nervous system balances stress and rest. Learning whether mere pictures move pain responses could reveal how much of chronic pain is driven by expectation.
plaw-107-177-2002: Passed in 2002, this federal law designates the Federal building and United States courthouse located at 501 Bell Street in Alton, Illinois, as the. Designations put names on the official map and into federal records. It stands as Public Law 107-177 of the 107th Congress.
plaw-107-206-2002: This 2002 law provides emergency supplemental funding for Further Recovery From and Response To Terrorist Attacks on the United States. Without it, the department cannot legally obligate funds. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-107-148-2002: Congress passed this federal law, the Radio Free Afghanistan Act, in 2002. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
plaw-107-192-2002: Passed in 2002, this federal law designates the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 2829 Commercial Way in Rock Springs, Wyoming, as the. Designations put names on the official map and into federal records. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record.
plaw-107-239-2002: In 2002, Congress passed a federal law to ratify an agreement between The Aleut Corporation and the United States of America to exchange land rights received under the Alaska Native Claims Set. Such transfers reshape who owns and manages the land going forward. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record.
plaw-107-322-2002: In 2002, Congress passed a federal law to extend the deadline for commencement of construction of a hydroelectric project in the State of North Carolina. The full text carries the binding legal details. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
