plos-pone-0357902:
Sitthatka Jaratsaeng and three colleagues test whether a phone selfie video can help assess Parkinson's disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The illness stiffens facial expression as well as movement, and clinic visits capture only snapshots. The team recorded forty participants with a standard smartphone front camera across several facial movement tasks, engineered measurements from the footage, and trained models to flag the disease and estimate its severity.

Smiling videos carried the most signal. The best classifier sorted patients from controls with accuracy near seventy-seven percent, and a companion model estimated standard motor scores, though with wide error margins. An explainability analysis showed the system leaned most on movements of the lips and mouth corners, which matches what clinicians watch. The authors present phone video as a low cost screening aid for remote follow up, not a stand alone diagnosis.
plos-pone-0355502:
H M Hamidur Rahman led a team of four authors who mapped rice planting in Bangladesh from space, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Bangladesh grows two main rice crops, called aman and aus, and knowing how much land each covers guides food planning. Clouds often block normal satellite views in the wet season.

Rahman's group used radar images from the Sentinel-1 satellite, which can see through cloud, paired with machine learning. Their maps estimate the area under each rice crop across the country. Timely crop maps help officials spot shortfalls early, plan imports or aid, and judge how floods or drought have hit the harvest that feeds most of the nation.
plos-pone-0357602:
Yufeng Chen, Hongyang Bian, and Yuye Li published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on spotting kidney injury early in sepsis patients. Sepsis often damages the kidneys quickly, but early signs are vague and outcomes are poor. The team built a dataset from two centers, an American public intensive care database and a Chinese hospital's records, extracting dozens of risk factors per patient as both text and numbers.

Their model reads those two streams with separate networks, one tuned for medical language and one for numerical patterns, then fuses them to classify risk. It performed steadily at the first center and carried over well to the second hospital, and the combined model beat versions using text or numbers alone. Training on two centers made it more adaptable to local patients. It is offered as decision support for earlier intervention, not a replacement for clinical judgment.
plos-pone-0357402:
Kathryn Biernacki and colleagues published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for VICTORY, a clinical trial testing whether magnetic brain stimulation can reduce opioid craving. People on buprenorphine, the standard medication for opioid use disorder, still drop out and relapse often. The trial will enroll up to one hundred twenty such patients and randomly assign them to real or sham stimulation aimed at a left frontal brain region involved in control and craving.

Treatment runs weekly for eight weeks, two short sessions per visit, with craving, use, and retention checked before, during, and after. Some volunteers will also have brain scans to test whether stimulation rewires connections between the target region and the brain's reward circuits, and whether those changes track with craving. Running at an academic center and a private clinic should show whether the approach works beyond a university hospital.
plos-pone-0355902:
Aly Ismailov and Maria Poptsova published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on a puzzle in glioblastoma, the deadliest common brain tumor. Where do its cancer-associated fibroblasts come from, when normal brain tissue has none?? Fibroblasts support tumors elsewhere in the body, so their apparent presence in brain tumors was controversial. The authors mined single-cell and bulk tumor data to trace the cells' identity. 

Gene activity formed a continuous spectrum from vessel lining cells through pericytes, the cells hugging vessel walls, to the fibroblast-like cells, pointing to pericytes as the source. Clean gene signatures let the team count these cells across cohorts. They were more abundant in the most aggressive tumor type and more abundant still after chemotherapy and radiation, one gene hinting at treatment adaptation. Patients with high fibroblast signature scores survived less well; these pericyte-born cells, the authors say, help remodel tumors after therapy.
plos-pone-0355202:
Jiye Lee and co-authors follow adults through repeated health checks to see whether cholesterol-lowering statin drugs shrink muscle over time. Muscle complaints are a known worry with statins, but long-term population evidence has been mixed. The team tracked limb and total muscle estimates from body scans in a few thousand adults over two years, comparing steady statin users with non-users.

At first glance, statin users lost more leg and arm muscle. Once the analysis accounted for body size and diabetes, which were both more common among users, the gap vanished for every muscle measure. Lee and colleagues conclude that statin use itself showed no clear tie to muscle loss in this group, a calming result for a widely used drug class.
plos-pone-0356802:
Hosein Ataei-Goujani leads a team publishing the protocol for a national follow-up cohort in Iran built on the country's twenty twenty-one risk factor survey. Diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and cancer cause most deaths in Iran, yet long-run outcome data after the pandemic are scarce. The cohort will re-contact survey participants to track deaths, disease outcomes, and, unusually, reproductive outcomes, since metabolic risk may shape fertility in a country worried about falling birth rates.

The design links a representative national sample to later health records under a fixed public plan. No results are reported in this entry; its purpose is to lock the questions and methods before outcomes are counted. Ataei-Goujani and colleagues aim to give Iranian policy a long view of risk rather than repeated snapshots.
plos-pone-0357202:
Subir Biswas, Yida Yang, and colleagues propose routing network data the way physics moves particles through a force field. Their 2026 paper introduces Particle Dynamics-based Routing. A network is treated as a landscape of gentle pushes. Each packet is launched with starting settings that steer it to its destination. It carries no directions in its header.

Because intermediate nodes need no destination tables, and headers never grow with network size, the scheme suits tiny Internet-of-Things devices with little memory. Simulations show forwarding stays light while trajectories remain controllable. Destinations stay hidden from nodes along the path. The authors frame the gravity-based version as a first proof that trajectory thinking can reshape routing design.
plos-pone-0357102:
Meselech Assegid Roro and colleagues audited 1,050 pregnancy records at three public hospitals in Addis Ababa to see whether screening for gestational diabetes follows the guidelines that recommend testing every pregnant woman. Their 2026 retrospective review recorded who was tested, when, by what method, and what the testing found.

Only about one woman in eight was screened at all, and almost all screening was triggered by risk factors rather than offered universally. Most tests came late, well past the recommended window in the middle of pregnancy, leaving little time to act. Among those tested, a striking four in ten actually had the condition. The authors conclude Ethiopia's hospitals are finding diabetes in pregnancy largely by luck and late, and urge universal, on-time testing.
plos-pone-0355602:
Didrik Ulleberg and four colleagues test whether fertilizer recovered from fish farm water keeps well in storage, in this 2026 study. Indoor fish farms that recycle their water produce an effluent rich in plant nutrients, and filtering it through reverse osmosis concentrates those nutrients into a liquid fertilizer. The open question was whether the product spoils over time unless it is heat-treated first.

The team stored both heat-treated and untreated concentrate in dark containers at room temperature for six months, sampling it regularly. Heat treatment lowered the starting microbe count, but both versions stayed chemically and microbiologically stable for the whole period. That means farmers can store the fertilizer for at least half a year without paying for pasteurization. The result strengthens the case for turning fish farm waste into a reliable crop input.
plos-pone-0354602:
Justin Lennon and three colleagues audit what British zoos actually hold, asking whether captive collections serve conservation, in this 2026 study. Zoos say they support biodiversity, but visitor income pushes them toward big, charismatic animals, and earlier work found a bias toward species that are not threatened. The team assessed the size and diversity of vertebrate populations across UK institutions, weighing both global threat status and local priorities.

Fish collections were the most diverse and amphibians the least. Populations of non-threatened species were more than double those of threatened species, and UK native and priority species made up only small shares of holdings overall. Still, zoos did keep threatened native fish and birds, plus a handful of species extinct in the wild. The authors conclude UK collections lean away from conservation priorities but hold real capacity to help native species.
plos-pone-0356602:
Jiwoo Shin and three colleagues compare three ginseng compounds for calming calcium overload in stressed brain cells, in this 2026 laboratory study. The pesticide rotenone, used to model Parkinson's disease, damages mitochondria and sends calcium flooding into both neurons and the brain's immune cells, the microglia. Blocking calcium channels outright is limited by heart side effects, so subtler modulators are attractive. The team exposed neuron-like and microglia-like cell lines to rotenone, with or without each ginsenoside.

Rotenone cut cell survival and raised oxidative damage in both cell types. All three ginsenosides, added just before, blunted the calcium surge and the damage markers. Their routes differed, though: one compound engaged several signaling pathways, while the other two worked mainly through a single enzyme pathway. The microglia leaned less on calcium channels than the neurons did. The authors say ginsenoside choice should be matched to cell type.
plos-pone-0356202:
Dávid Isztl and three colleagues benchmark artificial intelligence models for eye disease classification in this 2026 study, pitting compact general-purpose networks against a large foundation model built specifically for retinal images. Nine model configurations were trained identically across four tasks: sorting retinal scans into disease classes and grading diabetic eye disease, detecting glaucoma, and rating macular edema severity from photographs.

Pretraining on ordinary photographs helped every model. Small hierarchical models with a fraction of the parameters matched or beat the giants on three of the four tasks, with one tiny architecture ranking first on three. The big retinal foundation model won only the hardest grading task, where severe cases were rare in the data. The authors conclude small models suffice for most retinal benchmarks, reserving foundation models for skewed, difficult grading problems.
plos-pone-0355402:
Silvia Zanchi and seven colleagues probe how the senses share the work of keeping us upright, in this 2026 preliminary study. Eight healthy adults stood barefoot on a balance board while wearing a mixed-reality headset. The researchers varied what participants saw and played static or moving sounds. Sometimes they vibrated the Achilles tendons to scramble the body's position sense. Sway was measured by how predictable the body's pressure center remained.

Vibrating the tendons made sway markedly less predictable in all directions, while blurred vision tightened predictability in one plane only, suggesting stiffer control. Sounds seemed to do nothing behaviorally, yet a brain-inspired computer model of the same setup showed auditory input did shift predictability at the neural level, especially with moving sounds. The authors argue the model exposes sensory teamwork that behavior alone hides, though the sample is small.
plos-pone-0356102:
Thilagawathi Abi Deivanayagam and colleagues set out a plan to review youth involvement in action against fossil fuel harms. Fossil fuel production and use damage health, hitting disadvantaged communities and young people hardest. Their 2026 protocol describes a realist review, a method that asks what works, for whom, and in which settings.

No findings are reported, since the review is still to be carried out. Young advisers and an expert group helped shape the questions and will stay involved. The team will search published and grey sources and read the evidence through a structural racism lens. The finished review aims to show which forms of youth action can narrow health gaps linked to fossil fuels.
plos-pone-0356002:
Yue Su and co-authors searched for cell-death genes that connect bowel inflammation with thinning bones. Inflammatory bowel disease often arrives with osteoporosis, and the shared machinery is unclear. Their 2026 analysis mined public gene datasets for both diseases, then layered network and regression methods to narrow the field.

Two genes survived every filter and tracked with the course of both conditions. One builds a signalling protein tied to bone growth; the other is an inflammation alarm protein. Enrichment checks placed the wider gene set in immune and bone-relevant pathways. Su and colleagues present the pair as candidate bridges between the diseases, to be tested in laboratory and clinical work before any treatment claims.
plos-pone-0355302:
Pu Lei and co-authors compared mouth and gut microbes in mice made depressed-like by chronic social defeat stress. The mouth-gut-brain route is a newer suspect in depression biology. Their 2026 study confirmed the stressed mice avoided social contact, lost pleasure in sweet water, and showed despair-like behaviour across standard tests.

Mouth microbe communities separated clearly between stressed and control mice. Healthy controls carried more of a familiar mouth streptococcus and more of several gut commensal groups. Stressed mice carried a distinct signature in both sites. Correlation analysis tied particular microbes to particular behaviours. Lei and colleagues argue the mouth deserves a place beside the gut in depression microbiome research.
plos-pone-0354702:
Yudong Zhang and co-authors mine in 2026 almost fifteen years of visitor reviews for traditional earthen villages in Fujian, China, famous for huge round communal houses. Reviews came from two large travel platforms and were studied through common words, linked word networks, feeling scores, and changing topics over time. The villages remain lived in, not empty monuments.

Overall feeling was positive, shaped by scenery, village life, and service. Complaints centred on heavy selling, hard transport, tickets, guiding, and service management. Visitors judged the place through daily encounters as much as through famous views. The authors propose joining cultural care and service care as one task.
plos-pone-0354802:
Sara Jamali, Isaac Rahimian-Boogar, and Mojtaba Asgarabad present in 2026 a trial plan testing a mindfulness based therapy made for children from single parent families. The children, aged about ten to twelve, may show inward problems such as anxiety, outward problems such as acting out, or attention trouble. One group starts therapy at once, while the other waits and then crosses over.

Twelve weekly group sessions form the treatment, with checks running for a full year after. Standard interviews and checklists will track behaviour, feelings, attention, and mindfulness skill. As a protocol, the work states aims and methods and reports no results yet.
plos-pone-0353202:
Kosoku and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review of psychological distress in African adults with glaucoma. Glaucoma slowly steals vision, demands lifelong treatment, and can end in blindness, a heavy mental load. Yet no one had gathered the African evidence on how common that distress is, what drives it, or what support exists inside eye care.

The planned review will search major and African databases with no language or date limits. Two reviewers will screen studies separately, judge their quality with standard tools, and combine results statistically where the data allow, or in a structured narrative where they do not. The team aims to give clinics and policymakers a first map of the burden and of support services, so psychological care can be built into glaucoma treatment rather than bolted on. The protocol is registered in advance.
plos-pone-0354102:
Rabea Begum and three colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a study asking which physical tests forecast recovery from neck pain. Neck pain burdens millions, yet clinicians cannot reliably say whose pain will linger. About one hundred and fifty-six adults with neck pain will be recruited and examined with measures of impairment, physical performance, and everyday activity.

A year later the team will check pain, disability, and overall change, then test which baseline measures predicted them, using statistical methods that guard against overfitting. Knowing the few tests that truly carry information could spare patients pointless assessments and aim treatment at those headed for a hard year.
plos-pone-0352502:
Zafarullah and colleagues proposed a smarter way to route urgent health data in a 2026 study. Body sensors linked through the internet can flood a network during emergencies, causing vital messages to be lost. Older systems sort messages into broad queues but miss differences in how urgent each emergency truly is.

Their two-queue scheme places each message by sensor type and urgency, and lets a critical message jump right behind the one now being sent. Computer trials showed far fewer lost buffers and far fewer dropped emergency messages than two leading rival schemes. For remote patient watching, such gains could mean alarms reach care teams in time.
plos-pone-0353502:
Minchio, Vitali, and Scherer studied public childcare and childbearing across Europe in a 2026 paper. Many Europeans have fewer children than they say they want, and the gap is widest where family support is weak. The team linked regional childcare places for babies and toddlers with household records spanning 2005 to 2020.

Places with more public childcare saw higher chances of a first birth, and the link was strongest where provision had started low. Effects stood out most for employed women and those with less schooling. Second births rose too, though less evenly. The results suggest expanding early childcare can narrow the gap between hoped-for and actual family size.
plos-pone-0349702:
Fiorentino Polipo and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 on whether therapy training itself builds people skills in therapists. Warm, skilled responses to clients can be practiced and tested with standard tasks. The open question is whether formal therapy training grows those skills more than other people-focused studies do.

Under the plan, students will be tested at three stages, from entry to the end of a master's degree. Therapy students will be compared with nursing and teaching students, plus a group with less interpersonal training. If therapy students pull ahead over time, training deserves the credit; if all groups rise alike, the skills may come from general education and life.
plos-pone-0352702:
Lemos and colleagues set out a review plan in 2026 on low-level laser therapy for braces pain. Tooth straightening hurts after adjustments, and pain drives some patients to quit. The review will gather randomized trials comparing laser treatment with sham, nothing, or other relief methods.

Trials of special anchorage systems or elastic setups will be left out to keep comparisons clean. No date or language limits will apply. Laser therapy has few side effects, so solid proof of benefit would give orthodontists a drug-free option. Until the trials are pooled, claims for the lasers remain uncertain, which is exactly why the review is needed.
plos-pone-0353302:
Momo Irie and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study on whether how well a patient is nourished soon after a neck spinal cord injury predicts recovery. Malnutrition is common after such injuries. The team followed ninety-one patients admitted within three days of injury, scoring nutrition with three standard indices and measuring nerve function and independence again at six months.

Patients with better nutrition scores at four weeks regained notably more movement and independence by six months, in a graded pattern from poor to good nutrition groups. One index, built from albumin and blood cell counts, predicted recovery most strongly and held up after accounting for age, sex, and starting condition. The authors suggest early nutrition checks belong in rehabilitation planning after spinal cord injury.
plos-pone-0350802:
Arturo Ladriñán-Maestro and five colleagues test breathing low-oxygen air as therapy for sedentary older adults. Their 2026 pilot trial ran in a residential care physiotherapy setting. Sixteen volunteers split evenly between real treatment and a sham session. The real session cycled six rounds of low-oxygen air with oxygen-enriched air. The sham group breathed normal air, blinded. Heart rhythm patterns, blood pressure, and blood oxygen were measured before and after.

One session moved the needle. Heart rate variability rose in the treated group, signalling better autonomic control. A key rhythm ratio fell as well. Systolic and diastolic pressure and resting heart rate all dropped significantly versus controls. Blood oxygen was tracked alongside. Because the trial was tiny and measured only immediate effects, the authors frame it as a pilot. It justifies asking whether repeated sessions could help frail, inactive elders whose hearts respond sluggishly to daily demands.
plos-pone-0352202:
Peter Palenchar, working alone, studied how much gene activity varies from cell to cell in the mouse and in baker's yeast. Biologists use a measure called F star to capture that variation, hoping it can be read apart from how strongly a gene is expressed. Palenchar rechecked the measure with single-cell data from both organisms.

Variation and expression level turned out to be hard to pull apart, since the measure still tracks expression more than expected. Single-cell data also showed more apparent variation than pooled samples. One pattern held in both organisms, though: genes whose proteins have many interaction partners vary less. In the mouse, the steadiest genes clustered around protein building and related tasks.
plos-pone-0351702:
Missing dialysis sessions can be deadly, so Pramita Shrestha and colleagues asked patients in Nepal how important they judge sticking to treatment. Their 2026 PLOS One survey covered about two hundred eighty people on regular dialysis at two large hospitals during 2025.

Most patients rated adherence as highly important. Single patients scored higher than married ones, and patients whose parents came with them scored higher than those brought by others. The average age was near fifty. The authors read the pattern as a sign that close family support shapes how seriously patients take the schedule, and they suggest counseling that involves the family.
plos-pone-0349502:
Germany was split for four decades, and Enno Nowossadeck, Claudia Hövener, and Niels Michalski built suicide rate records for both halves from 1952 to 2022. Their 2026 PLOS One paper asks whether changes in disease coding or the 1990 merger of statistics faked jumps in the numbers.

Rates were assembled from many sources, split by sex and region. Statistical models that allow sudden jumps tested the suspicious years, including two coding changes and reunification. Rates swung up and down often, yet no clear method-made break appeared at those points. The authors conclude the long series is sound enough for studying real trends.
plos-pone-0351402:
Young adults with depression often wait years for a diagnosis, and Rena Xu and colleagues measured those delays in a national online American survey run in May 2025. Their 2026 PLOS One study gathered adults aged eighteen to thirty-five who had lived through at least one depressive episode.

Respondents reported when symptoms began, when a diagnosis arrived, and when treatment started, plus social support and group involvement. The team estimated how many never received a diagnosis despite symptoms, and what predicted longer waits. Older adults' delays are well documented; this study sizes the problem for the young, whose early treatment can change the course of adult life.
plos-pone-0337902:
Sasichakorn Wongsaichia and co authors surveyed just over six hundred shoppers in Thailand about green fashion made with buyers help. In joint design, shoppers share ideas early, so goods fit what people truly want. The survey asked whether that joint work changed how useful green fashion felt, how ready people were to adopt it, and how well brands seemed to perform.

Feeling part of the design raised both the felt benefits of green fashion and readiness to adopt it, and those steps in turn lifted brand performance. The chain matters for firms in growing markets. Inviting buyers in does more than improve a product. It builds trust and attachment that make a green brand look stronger and sell on more than price alone.
plos-pone-0351302:
Kimmo Sorjonen and colleagues warn about a popular panel model. The model tracks how two traits shape each other over time. It splits steady personal levels from change within a person. Simulations exposed a flaw. Shared outside factors can fool the model. It then reports cross effects that never existed.

The team also rechecked Dutch teen data. Topics were self esteem and problem eating. More than eighteen hundred teens took part. New runs gave shrinking, growing, and null effects. Results changed with each model setup. Past claims may rest on a maths artefact. Authors urge simple cross checks before any causal claim is trusted.
plos-pone-0335002:
Calista Ogechukwu Dozie-Nwakile and colleagues used a 2023 national survey in Lesotho to study smoking among three hundred and twenty six people with tuberculosis. Smoking worsens tuberculosis outcomes, and both burdens run high in poorer countries. Weighted survey models weighed sex, media exposure, alcohol use, stigma, mental health, and household traits against smoking status and daily versus occasional smoking.

About one quarter of patients smoked, most of them daily. Being male raised odds enormously, and alcohol use and no media exposure also raised odds clearly. Daily smoking showed the same pattern even more strongly. TB programmes in Lesotho should bundle quit help with alcohol care, and use media reach as a health channel.
plos-pone-0350402:
Yüksel Erkin and co-authors compared answers from three chatbots about myofascial pain syndrome in 2026. Patients increasingly ask such tools about the condition, which causes sore knots in muscle, but the quality and reading level of replies were untested.

Top search terms were put to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and two judges scored the answers for quality and trust, alongside six reading level formulas. All three wrote well above the sixth grade level advised for patient material. Scores also differed between tools. The finding is a warning that fluent medical answers can still be too hard, or too shaky, for patients.
plos-pone-0350102:
Xinglong Chen, Lingqiong Zhao, and Wenlong Luo studied a gene called PLXNB1 in allergic rhinitis smell loss in 2026. Many hay fever patients lose smell, and inflammation alone does not explain the molecular chain behind it.

Public data sets showed the gene running low in patients. Its level moved against inflammatory immune cell levels. In nasal cells and a mouse model, silencing the gene raised inflammatory signals through a known stress pathway, while restoring it, or a common allergy drug, calmed them. The gene emerges as a possible hub tying immune imbalance to smell loss, and a candidate drug target.
plos-pone-0350502:
Ibrahim A Naqid and co-authors surveyed medical students in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq about mpox, a virus that has recently spread to places where it was once rare. Future doctors will front the response to such outbreaks, so gaps in their knowledge matter. Their 2026 study questioned three hundred thirty students in Duhok Province using a structured survey on background, knowledge, and attitudes.

Only about four in ten students showed good knowledge, and fewer than half held a positive attitude toward control measures. Barely eight in a hundred had received any mpox training, and social media was the most common information source. Older students and those who already knew about smallpox scored better, while students relying on friends scored worse. The authors urge formal teaching on emerging infections during medical training.
plos-pone-0349402:
Weiyi Wang and colleagues followed four hundred five nursing interns in China across a ten-month internship to track two habits of mind. One was rumination, the tendency to replay worries again and again. The other was job embeddedness, how strongly a trainee feels tied to the job. Students answered surveys at the start, middle, and end of training.

Rumination fell steadily over the internship while attachment to the job rose. The cross-lagged analysis tested which change came first and which predicted the other. Results like these can guide schools and hospitals in supporting trainees, since a mind stuck on worry may loosen a new nurse's grip on the profession.
plos-pone-0348402:
Wenting Deng and colleagues explored whether a simple blood ratio can flag nerve damage in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy creeps in silently and cannot be reversed, so early warning signs are valuable. The ratio, platelets divided by the blood protein albumin, reflects inflammation and nutrition in one number. Patients from a Chinese metabolic clinic database spanning 2018 to 2023 were split by whether they had the nerve complication.

Statistical models tested the ratio against neuropathy while adjusting for other traits, traced whether risk rose steadily with the ratio, and measured how well the ratio alone separated the groups. A marker built from two routine lab values would cost nothing extra to compute, which is exactly the kind of signal busy diabetes clinics can use.
plos-pone-0345902:
Michelle Hirsch and colleagues interviewed younger and older adults about what curiosity means to them and how it feels, a basic question curiosity science has skipped. Definitions used by researchers may not match everyday understanding, and aging shifts emotions and goals in ways that could reshape curiosity. Both age groups described curiosity as joyful exploration.

Younger adults more often tied curiosity to a feeling of deprivation, to thrill seeking, and to being central to what makes us human. Older adults more often described its social side, curiosity about and with other people. Half of all answers fit none of the standard research categories, a sign that current frameworks miss how people actually experience one of the mind's basic drives.
plos-pone-0340602:
Ismail Marouani and co-authors modelled what it would cost to make green fuel gas for heavy industry by splitting water with clean power. Their system pairs solar panels and wind turbines with an electrolyser, batteries, and storage tanks, sized by computer to meet hourly demand. They compared the same setup with and without government support for building it.

Without help, the gas came out costly; with strong building subsidies, the price per kilogram fell by nearly half and the carbon cost dropped sharply too. Battery storage only made sense once its price fell a lot. Their results suggest that early public money, not just cheaper gear, is what can get clean hydrogen into factories soon.
plos-pone-0348602:
Nikhil Bhalla and Nupur Angrish mined the genomes of tuberculosis bacteria gathered from countries where the disease is common, hunting for hidden protein-making regions that standard catalogues miss. Lab strains differ greatly from the strains that actually infect people, and some of the difference may come from viruses that infect bacteria and swap genes. The team used a deep learning language model to predict these hidden proteins.

Most hidden proteins came from gene families already known for variety. One cluster stood out: its proteins matched no reference strain protein, yet carried virus-like parts and bits resembling primate DNA, a sign of past gene exchange. Computer folding checks found the shapes stable. The findings suggest viruses helped shape the tuberculosis germ's hidden toolkit.
plos-pone-0349202:
Zewdu Tessema and colleagues audited how well eighteen public health facilities in Ethiopia's South Gondar Zone keep track of medicines and supplies. Good records prevent stock-outs and waste; poor ones leave shelves empty or goods expired. The team checked stock cards against physical counts, reviewed ordering and reporting habits, inspected storage rooms, and interviewed staff about what goes wrong.

Emergency ordering was universal and rising, a symptom of planning failure. Fewer than one facility in five kept stock cards up to date, and average record accuracy sat near seventy percent, though vaccine cold storage scored well. Reports were sent often but were frequently incomplete or wrong. Staff blamed too few trained workers, weak training, and poor support systems. The authors call for investment in people and simple record discipline before fancier tools.
plos-pone-0349602:
Munachiso Iheme Ndukwe and colleagues compared two ways of diagnosing gynaecological tumours in women who also have fluid built up in the abdomen. One method draws cells from that fluid for inspection; the other threads a cutting needle through the vaginal wall under ultrasound guidance to snip a tissue core. Records from a Czech university hospital covered just over one hundred women, about half of whom had both tests.

The needle biopsy came out ahead on accuracy and on catching disease when present, and it was far better at ruling disease out when its result came back negative. Both methods produced usable samples at similar rates, and the needle caused bleeding in only one case. Agreement between the two diagnoses was moderate. The authors recommend the biopsy where it is feasible, keeping fluid testing as a fallback.
plos-pone-0348902:
Bin Du, Wei Qi, and Haibo Bai predicted how red sandstone weakens when it is soaked, dried, and soaked again in acidic water, then struck hard. Engineers need that strength value to judge tunnels and slopes in chemically harsh ground, but measuring it means smashing many samples. The team built a dataset of nearly six hundred dynamic tests and trained five ensemble learning methods on five easy inputs.

Two methods led the pack, with one slightly ahead, and an explanation technique ranked impact speed as the strongest influence on the result while the rock's static strength mattered least. The authors wrapped the winning model in a simple graphical tool so engineers can type in conditions and see the predicted strength. The reasoning stays exposed rather than hidden in a black box.
plos-pone-0349102:
Özgür Tutal surveyed four hundred and twenty-four teachers in southeastern Türkiye about a daily dilemma of centralised schooling. Should teachers follow the official curriculum exactly, or bend it to fit the class in front of them. Teachers reported their teaching beliefs, whether their drive comes from inside or from outside rewards and pressure, and how faithfully or flexibly they enact the set curriculum. Statistical modelling traced how these forces connect.

Teachers with student-centred beliefs leaned toward adapting the curriculum and were driven more by inner motivation, while traditionally minded teachers leaned toward strict adherence and outer motivation. Motivation sat in the middle of the chain: inner drive pushed toward adaptation and away from rigid adherence, outer drive did the reverse. Tutal concludes that reformers who want flexible teaching must feed teachers' inner motivation, not just rewrite the syllabus.
plos-pone-0342702:
Maria-Angeles Fuentes-Expósito and colleagues spent a year testing a phone app that helps breast cancer survivors track side effects and symptoms from home. Sixty-one survivors in a European project installed the Xemio app, logged how they felt, and later rated the experience, while the team compared app reports against standard quality-of-life questionnaires.

Forty-nine women used the app actively. Engagement started very high, with nearly everyone participating in the first three months, then faded to about a third by the last quarter, a familiar pattern for health apps. Usability scored in the excellent range, and most users said they would recommend it. The app also captured finer symptom detail than the questionnaires, especially for joint problems. The authors call it feasible and welcome, with adherence the challenge to solve.
plos-pone-0343902:
Comkrit Lomloy and co-workers search for drug pairs that work better together against the most common form of lung cancer. Single drugs often stop working as tumors resist them, but testing every pair in the lab is impossible. Their 2026 paper builds a computer method that spreads each drug pair's effects across a network of interacting molecules in a lung cancer cell line.

Grouping hundreds of pairs by shared effect patterns surfaced clusters rich in pairs that amplify each other. One shared pattern drove the boost in most of those clusters. That pattern centers on three linked growth pathways inside the cell. Naming the shared route gives drug hunters testable ideas for why certain pairs help each other and which pairs to try next.
plos-pone-0347602:
Yiwen Liu and co-workers hunt for blood protein clues that mark which vaccinated people later caught the Omicron variant of COVID-19. All volunteers were frontline workers who had never been infected and had taken a third vaccine dose. Their 2026 study compares blood samples from those who later had breakthrough infections with matched workers who stayed uninfected.

Out of thousands of proteins checked, twenty-eight stood out. Several signal proteins that draw immune cells were lower in the breakthrough group, while one growth signal for defender cells ran higher. The pattern suggests the virus slipped past first defenses while the body rebuilt its T-cell guard. Such markers could one day help predict who needs extra protection.
plos-pone-0348002:
Kaizong Ye, Zhen Chen, and Shanshan Zhao adapt a flexible statistics method for studying chemical mixtures in the environment. People are exposed to many pollutants at once, and their joint effect is hard to untangle. Their 2026 paper reshapes a tree-based Bayesian method so it can pick out harmful chemicals singly or in meaningful groups while still predicting health outcomes well.

In computer simulations, the adapted method matched or beat the field's standard tool at recovering true exposure patterns. It shone when chemicals were handled in groups. A case study on lasting pollutants and cell aging markers in national survey data showed the method working on real records. Cleaner mixture analysis helps regulators target the worst chemicals first.
plos-pone-0348502:
Valeria Ferrari and co-workers map the published evidence on direct harm that ships and boats do to whales, dolphins, and porpoises. Vessel traffic keeps growing worldwide, but knowledge of its effects is patchy. Their 2026 review screens tens of thousands of search hits down to five hundred sixty-eight documents and extracts more than six hundred fifty evidence records.

Bottlenose dolphins and humpback whales drew the most study, and tour boats were the most watched vessel type. North American waters dominated the record. Porpoises, beaked whales, African waters, and the open ocean were thinly covered. Many reports never even named the vessel type clearly. The map shows conservation science where to point its next surveys.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
As Israeli tanks ringed the Palestinian leader's compound in Ramallah, the Council called for a ceasefire. On 29 March 2002, it adopted Resolution 1402. Fourteen members backed it and none opposed it. Syria took no part in the vote. The text voices grave concern at suicide bombings in Israel. It also cites the attack on the Palestinian Authority's headquarters.

Both parties must move at once to a real ceasefire. Israeli troops must pull out of Palestinian cities, Ramallah included. The text repeats the demand made in Resolution 1397 days before. All violence, terror, and wrecking must stop at once. It backs the envoys then working to restart the peace track.

A bomb at UN headquarters in Baghdad pushed aid worker safety onto the agenda in 2003. On 26 August, the Council adopted Resolution 1502 without dissent. The blast a week before killed the mission's chief. Twenty-one others died with him. The attack is named in the text itself.

The Council condemns in strong terms the violence aid staff now face. Murder, abduction, and attacks on convoys all count. States must make sure such crimes do not go unpunished. All parties must let aid workers reach people in need in safety. The text pledges steps of its own as well. Host states should adopt the safety pact's key guards. The text still anchors debate on aid worker safety.

Two states share the Korean peninsula, but for decades neither sat at the UN. The Cold War kept both out. Each had a great-power backer blocking the other. That logjam broke in 1991. Resolution 702 passed without a vote on 8 August 1991. The Council had weighed each bid on its own.

The text backs both bids in turn. First comes North Korea, the Democratic People's Republic. Next comes South Korea, the Republic of Korea. The Assembly admitted both that September. The joint entry was a sign the Cold War was done. Rivals could now sit in the same hall. The door stayed open for talks, though the peninsula's split itself stayed firmly in place.

Southern Rhodesia's white rulers are pressed in Resolution 202, adopted on 6 May 1965 by seven votes to none with four abstentions. The General Assembly and its decolonization committee had repeatedly asked Britain, the colonial power, to free political prisoners, repeal repressive laws, and open political life. Two laws drew special dislike: the order law used to crush protest, and the land law that split farms and fields by race.

The Council endorsed those Assembly requests. It also flagged the danger in elections set for 7 May under a constitution most Rhodesians had rejected. The vote went ahead, the settler government won, and six months later it declared independence unilaterally, defying exactly the pressure this text applied.

Resolution 1602, adopted on 31 May 2005, extends the UN operation in Burundi as the country's transition nears its vote. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution by referendum in February. In May, the sitting president and the leader of the last big rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, signed a declaration in Dar es Salaam moving toward a ceasefire. The Arusha peace agreement of 2000 was the framework everything rested on.

ONUB's mandate was extended for six months, to December 2005. The Council assured all Burundian parties of its determination to see the transition end successfully through free and fair elections. It also restated support for the Arusha process and called on the parties to honor their commitments in full.

Resolution 502 was adopted in April 1982, right after Argentine armed forces invaded the Falkland Islands, called the Islas Malvinas in the text. The Council had already urged Argentina and the United Kingdom on 1 April to avoid using or threatening force in the area. Members said the invasion deeply disturbed them.

The Council rules that a breach of the peace exists in the region. It demands that fighting stop at once and that all Argentine forces leave the islands right away. It then calls on both governments to settle their differences through talks and to respect the UN Charter in full. The text became the Council's core legal statement on the opening of the Falklands War.

Haiti's fresh start under an elected government is the backdrop for Resolution 1702, adopted on 15 August 2006. A new president and parliament had been chosen in a calm transfer of power. The UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, was a key support. The government had approved a police reform plan and set social programs in motion, but gangs, weak courts, and crowded prisons still plagued the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH until 15 February 2007. It sets the force at up to 7,200 troops and 1,951 police, plus 16 corrections officers to help fix the prison system. It asks MINUSTAH to shift its disarmament work toward a community violence reduction program with jobs for former gang members and at-risk youth. It also urges fast completion of run-off and local elections.

Burundi's integrated UN office is renewed by Resolution 1902, adopted on 17 December 2009. The Palipehutu-FNL had become a political party under the December 2008 agreements, an electoral commission and revised electoral code were in place, and elections were due in 2010. Continuing rights violations, curbs on opposition assembly and expression, and violence by party youth groups remained concerns.

The Council extends the mandate of the UN Integrated Office in Burundi, BINUB, until 31 December 2010. BINUB must focus on the electoral process, democratic governance, peace consolidation, reintegration, and gender issues, and be ready to give the electoral commission logistical support at key moments. The government is pressed to protect the commission's independence, finish the disarmament and reintegration strategy, set up an independent national human rights commission, and end impunity. A briefing on the elections is due in May 2010 and a full report in November 2010.

Somalia's targeted sanctions are sharpened and the monitors renewed in Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. The Monitoring Group's July 2011 report documented embargo violations and revenue streams, drought and famine were worsening, and armed groups were obstructing humanitarian aid. The Council judged the designation criteria of Resolution 1844 (2008) needed reaffirming and strengthening.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirms the travel ban, asset freeze, and arms embargo reach those threatening the peace or the Djibouti process. They reach those violating the embargo, blocking humanitarian aid, recruiting children, or attacking civilians. Misappropriating transitional funds counts as a threat, and non-local commerce through Al-Shabaab-controlled ports counts as supporting a designated entity, so traders can be listed. It extends the Monitoring Group for twelve months with eight experts, tasked with investigating seaport operations raising revenue for Al-Shabaab. It exempts urgent humanitarian payments from the asset freeze for a year.

Security Council resolution 102 was adopted on 3 December 1953, by 10 votes to none with one abstention. It recommends terms on which Japan could become a party to the Statute of the International Court of Justice, without joining the United Nations. Japan would deposit an instrument accepting the Statute and the obligations of Article 94 of the Charter. It would undertake to contribute an equitable share of the Court's expenses. The General Assembly would assess that share.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme gets another six months of life here, in a text passed on 8 June 2000. The programme let Iraq sell oil under United Nations control while wide sanctions stayed in force. The money paid for food, medicine, and other basic goods for Iraqi civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council kept the rules first set in 1995 in force for 180 days from 9 June. Food, nutrition, and health kept first claim on the funds, with a fixed share set aside for the north of the country. The Council also pressed for fair sharing of goods in every part of Iraq and for stronger United Nations checks on the ground.

Fighting in eastern Ukraine had caused heavy loss of life when diplomats reached a deal in Minsk in February 2015. Resolution 2202, adopted on 17 February 2015, endorses that deal. The Council said the crisis in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions could only be settled in a peaceful way.

The Council endorsed the Package of Measures signed in Minsk on 12 February 2015. All parties were called on to carry it out in full. The package is attached to the resolution. It ordered a cease-fire from 15 February and a pullback of heavy weapons to create wide safety zones. The OSCE would monitor the cease-fire. The package also covered talks on local elections, a special status for the area, and an amnesty law.

A special mission sent to investigate Portuguese attacks on Senegal reported back in 1971. Portugal had refused to cooperate with the mission. Resolution 302, adopted on 24 November 1971, is the Council's response to that report. It follows up Resolution 294, passed the previous July.

The Council thanked the mission and welcomed its proposals. It condemned once more the violence and destruction carried out since 1963. Portuguese forces from Guinea-Bissau had attacked Senegalese villages again and again. Portugal was criticized for refusing to help the mission, and it was told to act at once to respect Senegal's land and people. The Council also called on Portugal to honor, without delay, the right of the people of Guinea-Bissau to govern themselves and be free.

Lesotho, a small country entirely surrounded by South Africa, paid a price for a brave stand in 1976. South Africa had closed several border posts with Lesotho. The closures were meant to force Lesotho to recognize the Transkei. The Transkei was a so-called independent bantustan created under apartheid, and Lesotho refused to recognize it. Resolution 402 was adopted by consensus on 22 December 1976.

The Council praised Lesotho's refusal. It endorsed the General Assembly's call for all governments to deny the Transkei any recognition. South Africa's attempt at coercion was condemned, and it was told to reopen the border posts at once. The closures were causing Lesotho urgent economic harm. The Council therefore appealed to all states for immediate aid. United Nations agencies were asked to organize financial, technical, and material help for the country.
un-sc-res-1402:
The second Palestinian uprising reached a grave point in March 2002. Suicide bombings had struck Israel. Israeli forces had attacked the headquarters of the President of the Palestinian Authority and moved into Palestinian cities. Resolution 1402 was adopted in March 2002, days after the two-state text, Resolution 1397.

The Council called on both parties to move at once to a meaningful cease-fire. Israeli troops were called on to withdraw from Palestinian cities, including Ramallah. Both sides had to work with the United States special envoy and others on the ground. Their first step was to carry out the Tenet security work plan in full. The Council also repeated the demand of Resolution 1397. All acts of violence had to end at once, including terror, provocation, incitement, and destruction.
un-sc-res-1502:
A bomb had destroyed the United Nations headquarters in Baghdad days before. On 26 August 2003 the Security Council spoke on the safety of aid and United Nations workers. It recalled the attack on the Iraq mission of 19 August. It voiced grave concern at violence against humanitarian staff in many places. Such attacks, it stressed, break the laws of war.

The Council condemns murder, abduction, hostage-taking, and attacks on aid convoys. It urges states to punish crimes against relief workers. It demands safe access for aid staff to all people in need. It also asks host countries to write stronger safety rules into their agreements with the United Nations.
un-sc-res-702: North and South Korea both sought United Nations seats in 1991. On 8 August 1991 the Security Council examined their applications separately. It recommended to the General Assembly that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea be admitted. It made the same recommendation for the Republic of Korea. The decision was taken without a vote. Both states joined that September. Their joint entry ended a long dispute over Korean representation.
un-sc-res-202:
Southern Rhodesia's drift toward a breakaway declaration met a warning on 6 May 1965. Elections under the rejected 1961 constitution were set for 7 May. The minority government was threatening a unilateral declaration of independence. The General Assembly and its special committee had long pressed Britain to free political prisoners and repeal repressive laws.

The Council noted Britain's stated terms for any grant of independence. It backed the majority view that Britain should call a constitutional conference of all parties. Britain and all member states were asked to refuse any unilateral declaration of independence. Britain had to act to prevent one from coming. No powers or armed forces were to pass to the Rhodesian government as it stood. The question stayed on the Council's agenda. The warning failed, and the Smith regime declared independence that November.
un-sc-res-1602:
Burundi's operation was extended as elections neared on 31 May 2005. The Arusha Agreement's transition was moving toward its close. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution in the referendum of 28 February 2005. On 15 May the president and the last rebel group's leader signed a Dar es Salaam declaration. They pledged an instant halt to fighting and a permanent ceasefire within a month.

The Council extended ONUB's mandate until 1 December 2005. All Burundian parties were called to work harder to make the elections a success. The Council looked forward to the Secretary-General's advice, due by mid-June, on the mission's future shape. He was to keep reporting on events as they unfolded. ONUB's work on a zero tolerance approach to abuse by its own staff was welcomed. The renewal carried the mission through the polls and the new government's birth.
un-sc-res-502:
Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands was met with a withdrawal order in April 1982. The Council's president had called on 1 April for both governments to shun force in the region. Reports then told of an invasion by Argentine forces on 2 April. The Council judged that a breach of the peace existed in the region of the islands.

The Council demanded an immediate end to hostilities. It demanded the immediate withdrawal of all Argentine forces from the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas). Argentina and the United Kingdom were called to seek a diplomatic answer to their differences. Both were told to respect the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter in full. The text gave Britain the legal ground it stood on through the war that followed. Argentina did not withdraw, and the fighting ended only with its surrender in June.
un-sc-res-1702:
MINUSTAH was renewed behind an elected government on 15 August 2006. Haiti had completed a peaceful move to elected rule, with a new president and parliament. The government's program covered modernizing the state and creating wealth. A social relief program answered the country's urgent needs. The Secretary-General's report of 28 July set out the mission's next phase.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate, as set by resolution 1542 (2004), for six months. The mission would keep a military part of up to 7,200 troops and a police part of up to 1,951 officers. Sixteen correction officers, seconded from member states, were authorized to help the prison service. Haiti's authorities were urged to finish the run-off legislative and local elections without delay. States were asked to supply well-qualified police. The Council restated its call for the mission to back the constitutional and political process and the rule of law.
un-sc-res-1902:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 1902 on Burundi on 17 December 2009. Burundi was preparing presidential and legislative elections for 2010. Rights abuses and limits on free assembly still drew concern. Youth groups tied to parties had clashed, and talks on justice for past crimes were under way.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Office in Burundi, called BINUB, until 31 December 2010. The office should focus on the elections, fair rule, peace, and the return of former fighters. The government must create fair conditions for the 2010 vote. It should also keep fighting graft, set up an independent rights body, and avoid steps that could raise tensions again.
un-sc-res-2002:
Somalia and Eritrea are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. Drought and famine were gripping Somalia that summer. Armed groups blocked aid and taxed trade through ports they held. Weapons kept crossing borders in breach of two arms embargoes.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council widens who can face travel bans and asset freezes. Recruiting child soldiers now counts, as do attacks on schools, hospitals, and civilians. Blocking aid and stealing public funds also qualify for listing. Trade through Al-Shabaab ports may count as backing a listed group. The Monitoring Group gains twelve more months, and urgent aid payments are shielded from the freeze for a year.
un-ga-res-president-george-w-bush-s-rema:
George W. Bush addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 12, 2002, and turned the hall's attention to Iraq. A year after the September 11 attacks, he warned of a grave and gathering danger from Saddam Hussein's regime. The speech began the public march toward the invasion that came six months later.

Bush lists Iraq's breaches of past Council resolutions on arms and terror. He challenges the UN to enforce its own demands or risk fading into irrelevance. He pledges to work with the Council while reserving the right to act alone. The address frames the case that shaped a war.
europmc-pmc10011802:
Yang and co-authors review AlphaFold2 and its uses in biology and medicine in a 2023 paper. AlphaFold2 is an AI system from DeepMind that predicts the three-dimensional shape of proteins from their building-block sequences. It does so with a level of accuracy that once took years of lab work for a single protein.

The review explains how the tool works and where labs now use it. Uses range from basic cell science to drug design and disease study. The authors also note the tool's limits. Readers get a clear tour of a landmark AI system.
europmc-pmc10200802:
Chen and a large team review macrophages in immune regulation and therapy in a 2023 paper. Macrophages are versatile immune cells that live in tissues throughout the body. They eat germs and dead cells, raise alarms, and help heal wounds, and they can switch between attack and repair modes.

The review explains how that switching is controlled and what goes wrong in cancer and chronic disease. It surveys therapies that reprogram macrophages or use them as drug carriers. The authors see these cells as both targets and tools in future medicine.
europmc-pmc10468402:
Li and co-authors showed in 2023 that chromosome errors in cancer cells drive spread through the immune system. Such errors, called chromosomal instability, scramble the number of chromosomes as cells divide. They had long been tied to metastasis, the spread of cancer to new sites. How much that link needs the immune system was unknown.

Errors trigger a DNA alarm, the cGAS-STING path, inside cancer cells. Li found that long alarm use rewires the cells and stirs stress in their inner stores. That mix makes the tumour zone friendlier to spread. Blocking STING or the stress path cut spread in mice with sound immune systems. Human breast cancer data showed the same marks in tumours that had spread.
europmc-pmc10622502:
Sun and co-authors reviewed smart nanoparticles for cancer care in 2023. These tiny carriers can sense body cues or follow them to a tumour. That skill marks them as a sharp tool for precise drug delivery. The review sorts the many carrier types now in work.

The list runs from polymer and protein carriers to gold, iron oxide, and carbon tubes. Sun shows how each is built and what makes it smart. Carriers can react to enzymes, acid levels, heat, light, or magnetic fields. Their surfaces can wear tags that grip tumour marks, such as folic acid. Loads range from small drugs to genes and even living cells. The team ends with a plan for AI-guided carriers.
europmc-pmc1082902:
Gould asks why tree leaves turn red in this 2004 review. Anthocyanins are the pigments, meaning colour-giving chemicals, behind the red and purple of autumn leaves. They were once seen as a wasteful flourish with no real use. Gould gathers newer work that points the other way, toward many protective jobs for these pigments.

The pigments help leaves cope with drought, strong sunlight, heavy metals in soil, leaf-eating animals, and germs, the review says. They soak up high-energy light, which shields the leaf's food-making parts from harm. They also mop up harmful oxygen-based molecules that can injure cells. Gould argues the pigments can be vital for a plant to survive harsh spots. He frames them as a multi-tool rather than mere decoration.
europmc-pmc11292402:
Yan and colleagues review the flexibility of macrophages in tissue repair in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are immune cells that adapt their behaviour to the tissue around them. Old teaching split them into two forms, M1 and M2. Recent work shows a spectrum of states beyond that split. Signal pathways, gene regulators, and chemical tags on DNA jointly steer which state a cell takes.

The review details the cascades involved, including Toll-like receptors, STAT proteins, nuclear receptors, and microRNAs. Two newer concepts get full treatment: metabolic reprogramming, where cells rewire fuel use, and trained immunity, a lasting memory-like tuning. In repair, macrophages coordinate inflammation, new vessel growth, and matrix rebuilding to restore tissue balance. The authors discuss harnessing this plasticity to speed regeneration. They frame control of these cells as a therapeutic lever.
europmc-pmc11294602:
An, Yu, Liu, Tang, Yang, and Chen review cell death driven by oxygen radicals, and its use against cancer, in this 2024 paper. Reactive oxygen species are reactive oxygen molecules made during normal cell work. In balance they aid signalling and immunity. When production outruns defences, oxidative stress damages fats, proteins, and DNA and can kill the cell.

That death takes several forms, among them ferroptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, each with distinct genetics and chemistry. Forcing it in cancer cells is an emerging treatment approach, the authors say. Five antioxidant proteins are named as key targets: SLC7A11, GCLC, GPX4, TXN, and TXNRD. Blocking them tips cancer cells into lethal stress. The review summarises the mechanisms of each death form and the drug opportunities they open.
europmc-pmc1239902:
Sporns, Tononi, and Kötter proposed mapping all brain connections in 2005. They named that full map the human connectome. No such map existed for the human brain at the time. Other mammals had partial connection collections, but nothing complete.

Knowing the parts and links of a network is key to grasping how it works. A full structural map would ground brain science and medicine. The authors lay out a plan to gather, store, and share the data. Sporns argues the map could explain how brain states arise. It could also reshape the study of thought and behavior.
europmc-pmc12687902:
GBD 2023 Cancer Collaborators estimated world cancer burden with forecasts in 2025. Many countries lack current cancer watch data. Estimates cover 47 cancer types or groupings. Data span 204 countries from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts to 2050.

Cancer registries, death records, and verbal autopsies fed the models. Mortality came from pooled models, and incidence from mortality ratios. Survival modeling produced prevalence and disability estimates. Risk-linked cancer burden was tracked across the same years. GBD 2023 Cancer Collaborators give planners a full global cancer ledger. Forecasts extend the same estimates through the year 2050. Risk-linked burden was tracked for the same years.
europmc-pmc1403802:
Bollback introduced a software tool named SIMMAP in 2006. Biologists use family trees, called phylogenies, to trace how traits change over time. Older tools relied on parsimony, which picks the path with the fewest changes. That shortcut can mislead, since it ignores doubt about timing, past states, and the tree itself.

SIMMAP maps traits with chance built in, a method called stochastic mapping. It samples many likely trees and histories rather than trusting one. Bollback notes that users can study trait links, shifts in form, and change in proteins. The tool turns a single fixed answer into a range of well weighed options.
europmc-pmc1435902:
Many adults struggle to read health leaflets, and clinics need a quick way to spot them. Morris and co-authors tested a one-question screen in 2006. The Single Item Literacy Screener asks how often a person needs help reading health papers. They checked it against a full reading test in 999 adults with diabetes.

About 17 percent had limited reading skill. The one question caught just over half of them, but ruled out the problem well. Most who screened clear, nine in ten, could read fine. Morris suggests the screen helps staff aim deeper checks at those most in need, though it misses some cases.
europmc-pmc1448202:
Drugs of abuse act on brain pumps that clear signaling chemicals after use. Han and Gu compared those pumps in humans and mice in 2006. The pumps handle dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, three key brain signals. Past lab reports of drug strength on them clashed by up to sixty-fold.

Han tested five drugs in one shared setup for a fair match. Cocaine blocked all three pumps at like strength. Methylphenidate hit two pumps hard but the serotonin pump weakly. Human and mouse pumps reacted much the same, within four-fold. The work gives drug studies a cleaner shared baseline.
europmc-pmc1550802:
Old antibiotics, dropped for their toxicity, are back in demand. Falagas and Kasiakou reviewed the safety of polymyxins in 2006. These drugs, found in 1947, kill tough Gram-negative bacteria that shrug off newer drugs. Fear of kidney and nerve damage had shelved them, except for cystic fibrosis care.

Old reports warned of frequent kidney and nerve harm, including blocked muscles. Fresh studies found kidney harm less common and less severe. Nerve effects were usually mild and faded when the drug stopped. No recent cases of breathing stoppage appeared. Falagas credits careful dosing and better intensive care for the safer record.
europmc-pmc1557402:
Some bacteria survive antibiotics by going dormant, not by resistance genes. Shah and co-authors found a way to isolate those persisters in 2006. They guessed the cells would make proteins slowly. Using E. coli that glows in step with growth, they sorted out the dim cells.

Those dim cells tolerated antibiotics that killed their kin. Their gene activity profile matched neither fast-growing nor starved cells. Genes for toxin-antitoxin modules, paired poisons and antidotes, were switched on. Shah concludes persisters form a distinct body state. That state, about one percent of a culture, helps explain why infections return after treatment.
europmc-pmc1564002:
Fish keep growing new eye cells all their lives. Raymond and co-authors mapped the stem cells behind that growth in adult zebrafish in 2006. True stem cells renew themselves, make many cell types, and wake after injury.

Two niches sustain them. One is a ring at the retina's edge, the ciliary marginal zone. The other wraps certain Müller glia, support cells inside the retina. In calm eyes those glia feed only rod cell lines. After injury they can rebuild many neuron types. Raymond likens the edge ring to stem cell niches in the adult mammal brain.
europmc-pmc1852402: qBase relative quantification framework and software for management and automated analysis of real-time quantitative PCR data. — a 2005 science paper on the qBase PCR tool. It manages the PCR data. The paper is the qBase guide: the findings on the PCR tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1919402: The social brain? — a 2005 science paper on the social brain. It asks if brains are social for labs worldwide. The paper is the social-brain study: the findings on social ills for labs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2042002: The cdx genes and retinoic acid control the positioning and segmentation of the zebrafish pronephros. — a 2005 science paper on fish kidney formation. It maps the pronephros control. The paper is the kidney-form study: the findings on zebrafish, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2174402: Endocrine-disrupting potential of bisphenol A, bisphenol A dimethacrylate, 4-n-nonylphenol, and 4-n-octylphenol in vitro: new data and a brief review. — a 2005 science paper on hormone-messing plastics. It grades the hormone-messing plastics for labs. The paper is the plastic-grade review: the notes on hormone ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2235902: Transcription factors bind thousands of active and inactive regions in the Drosophila blastoderm. — a 2005 science paper on transcription-factor binding. It maps the bound regions. The paper is the binding study: the findings on Drosophila, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2253602: The limits and intensity of Plasmodium falciparum transmission: implications for malaria control and elimination worldwide. — a 2005 science paper on malaria spread limits. It maps the transmission limits. The paper is the limit study: the findings on malaria, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2373902: Dynamic rerouting of the carbohydrate flux is key to counteracting oxidative stress. — a 2008 science paper on rerouting sugar flow. It finds the key rerouting. The paper is the rerouting study: the findings on oxidative ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2376102: A double-blind placebo-controlled, randomised study comparing gemcitabine and marimastat with g — a 2008 science paper on gemcitabine vs marimastat. It compares the two drugs. The paper is the drug-compare study: the findings on cancer, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2413402: Colorectal cancer stem cells are enriched in xenogeneic tumors following chemotherapy. — a 2008 science paper on colon-cancer stem cells. It finds the enriched stem cells. The paper is the stem-cell study: the findings on colorectal ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2428102: Oscillatory interactions between sensorimotor cortex and the periphery. — a 2008 science paper on brain-body oscillations. It maps the oscillatory interactions. The paper is the mapping study: the findings on cortex ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2486302: Proteomics reveals novel Drosophila seminal fluid proteins transferred at mating. — a 2008 science paper on fly mating proteins. It reveals the seminal proteins. The paper is the reveal study: the findings on Drosophila, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2564802: Efficacy and safety of abatacept or infliximab vs placebo in ATTEST: a phase III, multi-centre, — a 2008 science paper on the ATTEST trial. It tests the abatacept/infliximab efficacy. The paper is the trial study: the findings on ATTEST ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2643002: Sleep restriction increases the risk of developing cardiovascular diseases by augmenting proinf — a 2008 science paper on short sleep, sick hearts. It links the short sleep for labs. The paper is the link study: the notes on sleep ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2682202: Host cell factors in HIV replication: meta-analysis of genome-wide studies. — a 2008 science paper on HIV host factors. It reviews the genome-wide studies. The paper is the factor review: the findings on HIV ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2692002: Human fear conditioning and extinction in neuroimaging: a systematic review. — a 2008 science paper on fear conditioning. It reviews the systematic evidence. The paper is the fear review: the findings on human ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2701602: The role of anorexia in resistance and tolerance to infections in Drosophila. — a 2008 science paper on skipped meals and fly ills. It tests the skipped meals for labs. The paper is the meal study: the notes on fly ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2725302: rTMS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates dopamine release in the ipsilateral a — a 2008 science paper on rTMS and dopamine. It modulates the prefrontal release. The paper is the rTMS study: the findings on dopamine ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2738502: Vector competence of California mosquitoes for West Nile virus. — a 2008 science paper on West Nile vectors. It tests the mosquito competence. The paper is the competence study: the findings on vector ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2742902: Monitoring bacterial community of human gut microbiota reveals an increase in Lactobacillus in — a 2008 science paper on gut-bug head counts. It counts the gut bugs for labs. The paper is the count study: the notes on gut ills, filed here in full session today.
fossey-magie-assyrienne-1902:
Charles Fossey published his study of Assyrian magic in French in 1902. He gathered magical texts copied from ancient clay tablets. Transcription, translation, and commentary accompany each text in his edition.

The spells show priests battling demons with ritual formulas and sacred names. Illness, nightmares, and misfortune all had demonic causes in this world. Fossey explained the language and the rites for fellow scholars carefully. His study became a foundation stone of Mesopotamian religious studies. French Assyriology led the field in this period, and Fossey's book shows why. Anyone tracing magic's oldest written roots passes through his work.
boguet-discours-des-sorciers-french-1602:
Henri Boguet was a judge in Franche-Comté who tried and burned witches himself. His Discours des sorciers of 1602 turns that courtroom experience into a book. Boguet writes in French for the judges and officials who would follow him in such cases.

He describes sabbaths, marks, and confessions drawn from his own trials. Attached stands his Instruction for a judge in witchcraft matters, a working manual in miniature. The tone is calm, methodical, and utterly convinced. Firsthand persecution is here codified for later hands. Few books bring a modern reader closer to the mind of a witch judge at work.
nider-formicarius-latin-1602:
Johannes Nider, a Dominican reformer, wrote the Formicarius, the Ant-hill, around 1437. This text follows the Douai edition of 1602. Five books compare the church's enemies and its saints to the orders of an anthill, and the work became the first great demonological treatise of the witch-hunt era.

Nider collects tales of witches, heretics, and wonders from the Alpine world he knew. Heinrich Kramer quarried the Formicarius heavily when building the Malleus Maleficarum. Much of the Hammer's matter flows from Nider's hill. The dialogue form keeps the heavy doctrine readable. Anyone tracing the witch stereotype to its sources must pass through this book.
plos-pone-0004902:
Mireille St-Onge and colleagues studied impact of anti inflammatory agents on gene output in stimulated human neutrophils, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adenosine, prostaglandin E2, or increased cyclic AMP each elicit potent anti inflammatory events in neutrophils, inhibiting phagocytosis, superoxide production, adhesion, and cytokine release. Endogenous resolution pathways were unraveled by profiling how these agents reprogram gene output during active swelling.
