arxiv-2606-16002: One-class support vector machines learn to spot anomalies by training on normal examples only. This paper breaks that single model into an ensemble — a team — of simpler one-data models and combines their outputs. Published in Pattern Recognition, it aims to make anomaly detection more accurate and easier to understand.
arxiv-2606-16202: Soft things like cloth and dough are notoriously hard to simulate. EgoPhys learns physics models of deformable objects from first-person (egocentric) video — the kind a headset or robot camera records. The learned models generalize to new objects, aiming at robotics and AR researchers who need realistic soft-body prediction from ordinary footage.
arxiv-2606-16302: Flood maps save lives, and radar satellites like Sentinel-1 can see floods through clouds. This paper compares two AI approaches — CNNs and Transformers — for outlining flooded areas in radar imagery, with an emphasis on explainability: showing why the model marked each region. It targets remote-sensing researchers building trustworthy disaster-response tools.
arxiv-2606-16602: Neural networks trained to mimic physics simulations (PDE surrogates) often break when moved from simulation to reality. PhysGuard uses Fisher-guided gradient projection to keep the surrogate faithful to the physics during that sim-to-real jump. It targets researchers deploying AI surrogates for real engineering systems.
arxiv-2601-06802:
Ayman and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with doing more with less. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Although many Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have been developed for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Dialectal Arabic (DA).

Few studies have focused on dialect-specific implementations, particularly for low-resource Arabic dialects such as Sudanese. The work presents a comprehensive study of data augmentation techniques for fine-tuning OpenAI’s Whisper models and establishes the first benchmark for the Sudanese dialect. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06902:
Research by Stinne Zacho and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with santa clara 3D. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The work explores the potential of digital reconstruction and interactive storytelling to preserve historically suppressed sites. The main objective of an interdisciplinary team of data scientists from the MEMORISE project and associates of.

The memory association Asociación Recuerdo y Dignidad was to preserve the memory of the Francoist Santa Clara concentration camp in Soria. Spain, through the use of digital technology. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07302: Magnus Bertilsson and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with DIS dipole picture cross section in exact kinematics. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We implement a finite energy constraint in the dipole picture of deep inelastic scattering. By restricting the invariant mass of the produced partonic system by the virtual photon-target center of mass energy. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-08402: Donya Rooein and co-authors present PATS, a tutoring approach that adapts teaching to student personality. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that language models show promise as educational tutors. Different strategies benefit different personalities, though, and mismatches can harm outcomes. Current tutoring systems rarely account for student personality traits at all. PATS is personality-aware, matching strategy choice to the learner. Better matching could raise gains for students whom a single fixed style would leave behind, a common risk in automated tutoring.
arxiv-2604-01202:
Esakkivel Esakkiraja and co-authors ask when language models really decide in 2026. Their title plays on Descartes: Therefore I am. I Think. The question is whether a reasoning model thinks first, then decides.

Or does it decide first and then think afterward, they ask. Their paper presents evidence on that ordering inside chain-of-thought. Detectable, early-encoded decisions shape the reasoning that follows, they report. That finding matters for trusting long model explanations at face value. A chain of thought may justify a choice already made internally. Readers in AI safety get a concrete probe of hidden decisions. The work urges care before treating reasoning traces as honest windows.
arxiv-2601-06702:
Besher Hassan and Xiuying Chen present GRASP LoRA in 2026 for cross-lingual transfer. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts models to new languages with limited resources. Adapter pipelines usually choose a global prune ratio by grid search.

That practice is computationally expensive and development-set intensive, they argue. It repeats training, freezes sparsity, and misses fractional optima in ratios. Their method uses GRPO to guide adapter sparsity policy instead. A learned policy can pick sparsity per adapter, not globally. Cross-lingual transfer benefits when adapters keep the right connections per language. The paper promises cheaper searches for good sparsity settings. Practitioners adapting models to low-resource languages are the audience. Better policies mean more languages served at the same compute cost.
arxiv-2601-07902:
Alexey G. Gorinov and Alexander V. Zakharov compute the homology of spaces left after removing pieces of a torus. An affine subtorus is a shifted copy of a Lie subgroup inside the compact torus. Given finitely many such subtori and a prime p, they describe an explicit chain complex. That complex calculates the integral homology of the torus minus the union of the subtori. Binomial rings enter the construction. Their 2026 preprint gives the method.

Complements of toric arrangements appear in topology, combinatorics, and algebraic geometry. Their homology records holes and voids in the remaining space. An explicit chain complex turns that record into something computable. Local coefficients at the prime p refine the answer. The paper serves topologists who study arrangement complements. It supplies formulas where previously only case-by-case work existed.
arxiv-2601-08002:
Kathryn McKeough and colleagues build a Bayesian method for tracing the edges of faint X-ray sources. Mapping an extended source's boundary is a key step in studying its shape. Background contamination and statistical fluctuations make that hard, especially for low surface brightness X-ray images. Their three-step Bayesian procedure identifies boundaries of irregularly shaped sources. The method is named the LIRA-Ising model. Their 2026 preprint presents it.

A boundary drawn by eye varies between analysts and hides uncertainty. A Bayesian procedure states the boundary with its uncertainty attached. The Ising component favors coherent edges over speckled noise. Astronomers studying clusters, supernova remnants, and galaxies need such outlines. The author team spans astronomy and statistics departments. The paper serves both communities by treating a picture problem as an inference problem.
arxiv-2601-08602: Zishan Shu and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a vision model called WaveFormer. Top vision models, called Transformers, use attention to catch how parts of a scene link. But attention gives no firm account of how sense spreads. The authors treat each feature map as a signal in space. That signal shifts over an inner time tied to network depth. An underdamped wave equation rules how the signal shifts. The aim is a flow of features with a clear physical rule at its core.
arxiv-2601-09402:
Xinze Li and eight co-authors aim to give retrieval-augmented generation a better memory. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes structured knowledge pages that organize facts gathered during a search. Retrieval-augmented generation lets a language model pull in outside knowledge before it answers.

Some systems build knowledge step by step as they work on a query. The authors note that this stockpile often lacks a clear structure, which limits how complete and cohesive it becomes. Their contextual pages impose order on the gathered material. A tidier knowledge store should help models answer with broader, better-linked evidence.
arxiv-2601-09702:
Baruch Garcia takes a fresh look at a landmark result about the limits of proof methods. The 2026 arXiv paper revisits the Baker-Gill-Solovay theorem on relativization in complexity theory. Some separations, like P versus EXP, survive when all machines gain an oracle; others, famously, cannot be settled that way.

Garcia asks a specific point that he says was never proven outright: whether the Turing-recognizability of the acceptance problem relativizes. Diagonalization is the classic tool behind such results. Clarifying exactly what it can and cannot do keeps the foundations of complexity theory honest.
arxiv-2601-10102:
Viswonathan Manoranjan and Snehalkumar Gaikwad test if AI agents chase pay or play a role. Agents are now set in teams to do plan tasks. Each agent may get a role name and a job. It may or may not see the pay for each move.

The team asks which force wins. Does an agent pick the move with the best pay? Or does it act as its role would act, even at a cost? The test pits role pull against pay pull. The aim is to learn if teams of agents plan with care, or act from a script. That split shapes how such teams should be built.
arxiv-2601-10202:
Hongtao Li and co authors detect a heart fault from ECG traces. The fault is atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven beat. It raises the risk of stroke and heart fail. A firm test must work in one clinic and the next.

Past AI tests oft fail when the clinic changes. They may also waste facts in the trace. The team fuse two views of the trace. One view tracks time, one tracks tones. They train with a method that pulls like cases close. The aim is a test that is both strong and broad in use.
arxiv-2601-10302:
Yu. M. Poluektov sets a field as a chance height in a fast move frame. In quantum work, a field's height can code chance. Poluektov writes a fast frame law for a neutral complex field. The law is built so the height reads as a chance weight.

From it, he gets a flow rule for the chance weight. The weight is kept as the field moves. He finds two kinds of waves in the field. Both have plus energy, but their spread rules part. From a Lagrangian form, he draws the kept laws of the field. The work reframes field laws in chance terms.
arxiv-2601-10502:
Jiaze Li, Michael Schaub, and Leto Peel find trade offs in group hunts on hypergraphs. A hypergraph links sets of nodes at once, not just pairs. Groups in such a net are sets that link more in than out. Past graph tools do not map clean to this case.

Sets in a hypergraph come in many sizes. A large set can span groups in ways a pair can not. That makes group sense less clear. The team work out the trade offs this brings. They show what must be lost or gained in each call. The work sets a base for group tools on rich nets.
arxiv-2601-10802:
Gerhard Krumpl, Henning Avenhaus, and Horst Possegger present ICONIC-444, a dataset of 3.1 million images for out-of-distribution research. Progress in spotting out-of-distribution inputs has been held back by data. Few sets offer clear OOD categories at graded difficulty, from near to far. Fewer still serve both fine- and coarse-grained vision tasks.

ICONIC-444 is built to fill that gap at scale. Graded categories let researchers test where a detector starts to fail. Fine labels test whether models notice subtle shifts, not just gross ones. A shared, large testbed can make results across papers comparable at last. The dataset targets safer vision systems that know when they are out of their depth.
arxiv-2601-10902:
James Freeburn and a large team present the first optical data release of the Deeper, Wider, Faster programme. The fast sky, events that flare and fade in under an hour, is poorly charted. With the Dark Energy Camera, the programme scans a unique space: deep images, reaching a median of about magnitude 22.2, taken at minute cadence.

Fast cadence catches supernovae in their first hours and other quick transients that slow surveys miss. A public data release lets the whole field mine those catches. The paper documents what the release holds and how it was built. Time-domain astronomers gain a resource for the fastest changing sky yet surveyed in depth.
arxiv-2601-12202:
Sambit Das and Vikram Gavini explain a gain in ductility in magnesium alloys via large ab-initio calculations. Magnesium is the lightest structural metal, yet its low ductility limits use. Recent work hints that dilute alloys gain ductility from solute shifts in dislocation core energy.

The key shift is in pyramidal screw dislocations, which can then cross-slip twice and spread strain. Their large first-principles runs test that story. A firmer story could guide alloy design for cars and planes. Light yet ductile alloys save fuel at scale.  Their runs are large scale by the norms of the field.
arxiv-2601-11502:
Natalia Zawadzka and six coauthors read fingerprints of a charge density wave. Their 2026 preprint studies NbTe4, a near one-dimensional crystal. A charge density wave is an ordered state of conduction electrons. It comes with a periodic distortion of the crystal lattice.

Raman scattering suits the hunt for such modulations well. Light scattered off the crystal reports its vibration modes. At 5 K, the spectrum shows 25 phonon modes in the work. Resonant enhancement makes those faint modes stand out. The mode set acts as a fingerprint of the wave state. It can track how the ordered state forms and shifts.
arxiv-2601-11602:
Sungwoo Kang studies the physics of price discovery in markets. The 2026 preprint tracks how an informed signal travels and breaks. A prior 2025 finding set the stage for this work. Market cap normalization isolates a pure directional signal there.

That signal reflects informed trading in the market. Kang asks how it is transmitted through price action. He also asks how it breaks down under stress. Retail herding is the breakdown case in the title. When crowds herd, the clean signal can fail at once. Deconvolving information and volatility is the method's core. Such work speaks to traders who read order flow signals.
arxiv-2601-11702:
Yu Yang, Ig-Jae Kim, and Dongwook Yoon evaluate AI compliance across many policies. Their 2026 preprint names the framework PASTA. AI compliance grows critical as systems spread everywhere. Policies multiply fast, and checking them all is costly.

Resource-constrained practitioners often lack policy expertise. Existing approaches address one policy at a time. Multi-policy checks then cost too much for small teams. PASTA is a scalable framework for the joint task. It evaluates compliance against many policies in one pass. Shared work across policies cuts the total burden. The tool serves builders who must answer to many rules.
arxiv-2601-13302:
Lizhou Sha and co-authors count how often hot Jupiters have close planet mates. A hot Jupiter is a huge gas world in a tight, fast orbit. More than five hundred such worlds are firm finds, with about two thousand more in wait. Just ten are known to have a close mate.

That count speaks to how such worlds moved. A mate could not live through a wild, high stretch swoop to the tight orbit. So hosts with mates must have slid in through a disk or formed in place. By count of mates in a clean way, the team helps split which path most hot Jupiters took.
arxiv-2601-13402:
Patrick De Visschere reviews how colour gaps in theory are matched to colour gaps seen by eye. A line element is a local rule that states how far two near hues sit for the human eye. Tests yield real gaps for pairs of hues. Many scores have been used to judge how well a rule's gaps fit the seen gaps.

Those scores can be skewed by how test hues were picked. Pick of paths in a hue point can be loose and one sided. De Visschere joins the scores over a full ellipse or ellipsoid in place of a loose pick. That full join wipes the pick bias. Colour staff gain a fair way to rank hue rules.
arxiv-2601-12402:
Aleksandra Jamroz, Patrycja Wysocka, and Piotr Garbat review systems that read emotion from faces. Such systems play a role in how humans and computers interact. The range of methods in the field is vast. That spread alone makes a close review of the work worthwhile.

The team pick out three of the most notable and best solutions for close study. They also pick three datasets that stand out for range and size. With those in hand, they probe where face based emotion systems fall short. Weak spots can range from odd lighting to faces that do not fit the norm. A clear map of flaws helps builders know what to fix first.
arxiv-2601-12502:
Mikhail Gennadievich Belov and five co authors study how to reconstruct a quantum channel from data. A quantum channel describes how a quantum state changes as it passes through a device or medium. The team consider learning that channel from a sample of classical data. That is, the inputs and outputs seen are classical records, yet the object to learn is quantum.

Their tool is semidefinite programming, a class of optimization with strong solvers. Framing channel learning as such a program gives the task a clean, tractable form. Exact channel knowledge matters for calibrating quantum hardware. It also matters for checking that a device does what its maker claims. The work adds a method to the quantum tomography toolkit.
arxiv-2601-12702:
Work with no author named in the record studies Igusa Todorov properties under recollements of abelian categories. A recollement glues two categories into a larger one in a structured way. Igusa Todorov properties measure how complex the homological structure of a category is. The work asks how these properties behave when categories are glued.

In particular, it relates the Igusa Todorov distances of the parts to the whole. Applications are given to Artin algebras, a central class in representation theory. Morita context rings get special attention as a test case. Results of this kind let algebraists transfer knowledge between categories. They show which homological traits survive gluing and which do not.
arxiv-2601-13002:
Chen Zhao and six co authors present a theory of the correlated Hofstadter spectrum in magic angle graphene. Magic angle twisted bilayer graphene hosts correlated Chern insulator states in a magnetic field. Those states have been intensively studied in experiments. A simple and clear understanding of their origin is still lacking, the team note.

They propose a unified theoretical framework for these states. The framework successfully explains most experimental observations, per the abstract. Hofstadter spectra arise when magnetic flux and lattice period compete. Adding electron correlation makes the picture far richer. A unified account would anchor a flagship material of modern condensed matter physics.
arxiv-2601-13802:
Yushen Chen and co-authors lay the base for Arabic speech synthesis across many dialects in 2026. Arabic dialects vary much in sound and word choice. Research on speech synthesis for them lags, in part from their complexity. A lack of standard data, benchmarks, and eval rules pushes teams to safer topics.

Their project, Habibi, aims for a unified model of Arabic dialects. One model for many dialects could serve far more speakers than single-dialect tools. Open-source release lets other teams build on the base. Good speech tools in one's own dialect aid access and pride.
arxiv-2601-14102:
The CMS team at the LHC measures a rare particle process and hunts for new couplings in 2026. They study production of a Z boson with a high-energy photon in proton-proton collisions. The Z decays to two neutrinos, which escape unseen. Data came from collisions at thirteen TeV during 2016 to 2018.

The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 138 inverse femtobarns. They report the fiducial cross section for this production. They also search for anomalous neutral triple gauge couplings, signs of new physics. Any crack in the expected couplings would point beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2601-14302:
Jinwei Hu, Shiyuan Meng, Yi Dong, and Xiaowei Huang study attack tests for image systems in this 2026 paper. The setting is image transmission and processing in resource-critical work. There, adversarial perturbations, small crafted changes to an image, can break mission-specific object classification. Tests must check that risk before deployment.

Current test methods cost too much compute. They process each frame in full and perturb whole images. That load is impractical when huge image streams need fast checks. The team's method, DDSA, is a dual-domain strategic attack. Its stated aim is spatial-temporal efficiency, so robustness tests can run at real scale.
arxiv-2601-14402:
Michael Cui, Chenxin Dai, Yixuan Even Xu, and Fei Fang study peer review logistics in this 2026 paper. Assigning papers to reviewers is a central challenge for large academic conferences. Program chairs must balance competing goals. They want strong reviewer expertise on each paper. They also want diversity and robustness against strategic manipulation.

Doing all that at modern conference scale is hard. Thousands of papers and reviewers must be matched at once. The team presents a unified framework for the task. It is built to be both scalable and robust. Readers get a method aimed at fair, sound matches when the numbers grow huge.
arxiv-2601-14802:
Donnate Hooft and four co-authors improve 3D medical image segmentation in this 2026 paper. Their method, LocBAM, advances patch-based image segmentation by integrating location context. Patch-based methods cut a scan into small cubes and label each one. A cube alone can be ambiguous: the same texture may be healthy in one organ and a tumor in another.

Location context tells the model where in the body each patch sits. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off just as it introduces patch-based methods. The title carries the full claim, though. Readers get a segmentation design that uses anatomy as a prior, so local labels respect the map of the body.
arxiv-2601-15502:
T. Troncoso Enríquez and three co-authors study red blood cells under light forces in a 2026 arXiv paper. They use evanescent waves, which arise in total internal reflection. The setup pairs a 1064 nanometer laser with a dual-chamber prism. With it, they track how red blood cells move. The key question is how glucose levels change that motion.

Automated tracking does the measuring work. The team uses the TrackMate tool to follow cell paths. They analyze more than 60 sets of trajectories. Glucose matters because cell stiffness and motion shift with it. A method that reads those shifts with light could aid blood research. It may also point toward new ways to probe cell health without touching the cells.
arxiv-2601-15702:
K. Guratinder and four co-authors study a two-dimensional magnetic material in a 2026 arXiv paper. The material is Cr7Te8, grown by vapor deposition. It shows unusual Hall effect behavior as temperature changes. At room temperature, it displays an anomalous Hall effect. On cooling, the Hall resistivity flips sign. At low temperatures, it shows a peak. The measured films are hexagonal in structure.

The paper focuses on spin reorientations inside this material. A spin reorientation is a shift in how magnetic moments align. Such shifts can explain swings in the Hall signal. The material is also described as structurally metastable and disordered. Those traits complicate the picture but make it richer. Thin magnetic films like this are candidates for future devices.
arxiv-2601-15802:
Alexandre Albore, Humbert Fiorino, and Damien Pellier plan stealthy navigation for underwater drones in a 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous unmanned underwater vehicles work without support vessels. They also work where satellite navigation cannot reach. Such independence matters in coastal zones with no surface access. It matters even more in restricted or dangerous areas. There, stealthy navigation is required, not optional.

Their solution is beacon based, per the title. Beacons placed in the area give the vehicle reference points. From them, it can fix its position without surfacing for a satellite signal. Staying submerged keeps the vehicle hidden and safe. The project drew funding from a French national source, per the record. Military and civilian users share the need for quiet, self-reliant navigation.
arxiv-2601-15902:
P. Dasgupta and D. Gangopadhyay work on safer teleportation with deformed quantum states in a 2026 arXiv paper. Teleportation moves a quantum state by using entanglement plus classical messages. Its safety matters if it carries sensitive data. The authors use q-deformed algebras as their tools. Their entangled states come from q-deformed harmonic oscillators. These states are not maximally entangled, yet they serve the protocol well.

The deformed states expand into standard oscillator states. The expansions carry free functions of the parameter q. That freedom is a knob for safety: the sender can vary the deformation. A spy then faces a moving target. The authors claim stronger cryptographic safety for the scheme. Quantum links need such knobs, since protocols must stay ahead of attack methods.
arxiv-2601-16002:
Xiang Zhang, Chen Sun, and Fuxiang Li engineer a quantum relaxation quirk in a 2026 arXiv paper. The quantum Mpemba effect is counterintuitive. A state farther from steady state can relax faster than a closer one. The authors propose building this effect with the Liouvillian skin effect. That effect arises in open quantum systems. In their open quantum chain, the skin effect sorts states by position.

States localized at the left or right edges relax in distinct ways. One side decays algebraically, the other exponentially. Choosing only the spatial profile of the start state can thus realize the effect. Simple control is the appeal: no complex driving needed. Open-system quirks like this may serve quantum devices, where relaxation speed is a design parameter.
arxiv-2601-14902:
Huanhuan Shi, Qili Li, and a large team study a layered crystal called NbSe2. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how its electrons settle into ordered states. In thin layers, charge can form a wave-like pattern, and the crystal can also carry current with no loss.

Atom-thin layers show this physics well but are hard to probe. They are tiny and react fast to their surroundings. The team slips organic ions between the layers of a bulk crystal by an electric method. That bulk form then acts like a single thin layer, but is far easier to study.
arxiv-2601-15002:
Wen Chen, Zhan-Jiang Lian, and a team of co-authors work on the math of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with angular momentum projection. The step builds nuclear wave functions that carry a clean, fixed spin.

The standard route projects a reference state for the whole nucleus at once. The authors break a projected wave function into parts instead. Their decomposition reworks how the basis of states is built. Work like this helps theorists compute what a nucleus does while keeping its spin exact and clean at each and every step.
arxiv-2601-15102:
Johannes Meuer, Maximilian Witte, and co-authors build a faster stand-in for climate models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Earth system models that run at kilometer scale. Such models catch local climate change well, but they cost a huge amount to run.

Their output can reach petabyte scale, which limits uses such as risk assessment. The team presents the Field-Space Autoencoder. It is a climate emulation framework built on spherical compression. The model squeezes global fields down and rebuilds them, so many more runs become cheap enough to use in practice.
arxiv-2601-16202:
Nguyen Thi Phuong and Nguyen Tat Thang map gas and dust in a young pair system. Their 2026 preprint uses ALMA views of the AS 205 system. The views span dust glow at two wave lengths. They also span line glow from CO and its rare kin forms. Sharp views reach scales of tens of AU in the disks.

The maps show dust spread that is not the same on each side. Gas lines trace how the pair disks move and mix. Lopsided dust hints at pull from the pair mate or a young world. Such maps guide tales of how pair stars shape world birth. The work joins dust and gas views in one study.
arxiv-2601-16402:
Shubham Parashar and Michael Fogler study flow round a thin spot in a 2D electron gas. Their 2026 preprint deals with flow in a strong field. The thin spot is a dip in charge count with a tail. That tail fades by a power law with a set grade. Past a grade of two, the tail is thin yet still shapes flow.

The pair split flow acts in thin and wet like zones. Each zone has its own rule for how flow bends round the dip. Such bends shape what probes read in Hall tests. Clear rules help read dip traits from flow maps. The work is a pure theory study of field flow.
arxiv-2601-16702:
M. N. M. van Lieshout takes on a hard choice for rescue chiefs. Crews and trucks must sit where they can help most. Past crash and call logs show where need tends to rise. Their 2026 preprint turns those logs into a place plan. The plan solves two linked tasks in a row.

First, trucks are set to posts by the log-based plan. Next, crews are set to trucks in the best match. Math proofs guard both steps of the plan. Such plans can cut wait times for aid. They also help chiefs use scarce staff with care. The work was penned in honor of Joseph Glaz.
arxiv-2601-16902:
Douglas Farenick, Roghayeh Maleki, Sofia Medina Varela, and Sushil Singla study forms built from group rules. Their forms come from free joins of two-cycles. One join pairs a 2-cycle with a k-cycle. The next joins d two-cycles in a row. Maps of these forms show their shape in a wild math world. That world is called noncommutative geometry.

Their 2026 preprint reads such maps to learn the forms' traits. Cubes and prisms in that world act in odd ways. Plain cubes gain new traits when swaps stop commuting. Such work feeds quantum math and signal work. It also grows the map of wild forms.
arxiv-2601-17302:
John H. J. Einmahl and Yi He work on confidence intervals for quantiles of mixed data. A quantile marks a cut point in data, like the median. When data come from mixed groups, sample quantiles can vary less than in the plain same-source case. That fact has been known for some time. What was missing is an interval that stays correct in large samples.

The authors give a new estimator for the reduced variance. With it, they build intervals that are correct as samples grow. Honest intervals matter in risk, health, and pay studies. Mixed data is the norm there, not the odd case. Their method lets analysts claim the gain that mixing truly gives.
arxiv-2601-17502:
Emmanouil Georgios Lionis, Craig Macdonald, and Sean MacAvaney show new tools in PyTerrier. PyTerrier is a declarative frame for search experiments. Pipelines chain steps like retrieval, reranking, and scoring. The demo adds ways to inspect those pipelines from code. It adds views that draw the pipeline for the eye. It also links pipelines to other tools.

The link uses the Model Context Protocol. That lets AI tools and apps call pipeline steps. Clear views help teams debug search systems fast. Shared links cut the glue code each lab writes alone. The work serves search research at large. It makes pipelines things you can see, test, and reuse.
arxiv-2601-17702:
Qingsen Ma and co-authors present S3-Attention for long-context inference in language models. Full context makes the KV cache grow in a linear way. Offloading to outside retrievers saves memory. But retrieved passages can match words while missing the true causal thread. S3-Attention turns memory-bound inference into a streaming task. Retrieval is endogenous, drawn from the model's own attention.

Attention-aligned picks should track what the model truly needs. That keeps long reads exact on a fixed memory budget. Book and code length inputs are the target use. A streaming design also fits live chat with long histories. The work joins memory and attention in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17802:
A team of authors presents a computing framework for finding a hard-to-see kind of tumor region in brain scans. Their 2026 preprint deals with regions that are dense with cells but do not light up under contrast dye. Doctors call them non-enhancing hypercellular regions. Finding them in routine MRI scans is an unmet need in brain tumor care, and the stakes for treatment plans are high.

The framework builds maps that show the chance that each spot in a scan is such a region. It draws on several network designs to cope with the wide range seen in real clinic data. Maps of this kind could guide doctors as they plan surgery or therapy. The work aims for tools that hold up outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-18202:
Fangyuan Xu and co-authors generate training data for deep search agents, with execution feedback in the loop. Their 2026 preprint presents SAGE. Deep search agents answer hard questions by reasoning across many documents. They could speed up information seeking a great deal. But human annotation for such training is far too costly to gather at scale. Synthetic data is the natural answer, if it can be made good enough.

SAGE is steerable, so data can be aimed at weak spots. Execution feedback checks whether a generated task and answer actually work. That check filters out junk that pure generation would pass. Better agent training data means search assistants that fail less on hard questions.
arxiv-2601-18902:
Jiaming Fan and five co-authors look at how to train small draft models that speed up large language models. In this trick, called speculative decoding, a small model guesses the next words and a big model checks them. The draft model needs a large training set, which costs time and compute.

The team takes a data first view and finds that not all training samples help the same amount. Flat tokens, in their words, prove worth more than the rest for how often guesses get accepted. Picking the right samples could let draft models train on less data and still speed up text output well.
arxiv-2601-19002:
Yihan Fang studies a hidden snag in a method that maps DNA methylation from scarce samples. The method reads methylation in low input and broken samples, even free DNA in blood. Its lab steps add tails to DNA strands, which blurs the line between real sequence and added bits.

Cutting reads back to size, called trimming, then varies a lot from one pipeline to the next. Fang asks what limits trimming itself has in this setting, past which no tool can do better. Knowing the hard limit helps labs judge when odd results come from the method, not from the sample.
arxiv-2601-19202:
Chi Zhang and five co-authors test whether false words can outshout true pictures in visual models. Vision language models do well on visual question tests, but their strength when text misleads them is little studied. Past work on falsehood focused on text only worlds, leaving the clash between senses untested.

The team builds a test set, ConText-VQA, where the text and the image tell opposed stories. It shows how the models settle the clash: sight or words. A model that drops what it sees for what it is told would fail in news, medicine, and safety checks where captions can lie.
arxiv-2601-19302:
Natapong Nitarach, Pittawat Taveekitworachai, and Kunat Pipatanakul prompt language models to race through math with equations first. Prompt styles like chain of thought lay reasoning out in words, while others write code. Applied math in finance, physics, and cryptography often turns on recalling or deriving the governing equation, a step those styles do not stress.

Their style, Formula-One prompting, makes the equation the spine of the solution. The model adapts its reasoning around the formula it must use. For problems where one right equation decides all, putting it first could cut the wandering that wordy reasoning invites.
arxiv-2601-19402:
Amit Singh Bhatti, Vishal Vaddina, and Dagnachew Birru route queries across many language models with service promises attached. Live deployments serve mixed workloads where cost and quality needs vary by customer tier, hour, and how critical the query is. Serving systems take latency promises directly, but model routers do not.

Operators must tune router knobs offline and guess the accuracy that will result, since knobs and outcomes link in indirect ways. Their system, PROTEUS, uses Lagrangian reinforcement learning to route with the promise in the loop. Routers that honor stated service levels would make multi model serving far easier to run.
arxiv-2601-19502:
Shuning Zhang and nine colleagues tackle a privacy problem created by smart glasses. The glasses can sense their surroundings at all times, and their front cameras record what the wearer sees. In a home, that camera may catch private objects and family members who never agreed to be recorded. Simple on-off permission switches cannot handle such shifting, context-based risks.

Their answer is VisGuardian, a light control method built around groups. The idea is to set privacy rules for sets of people and places, not just one user at a time. A home is full of shared spaces and daily routines, so rules need to fit that setting. The work points toward camera controls that respect the people nearby, not only the person wearing the glasses.
arxiv-2601-19702:
Helin Wang and six colleagues build a judge for machine-separated audio. Audio separation splits a mixed recording into its sources, such as one voice from a crowd. Judging the quality of the split is tricky. Standard metrics often disagree with what human listeners prefer, and they usually need the clean original signals for comparison.

Listening tests by people remain the gold standard, but they are slow, costly, and hard to scale. The authors present SAM Audio Judge, a multimodal framework that scores separation the way people perceive it. A reliable automatic judge would speed up research on hearing aids, transcription, and music tools. The work tries to close the gap between lab numbers and human ears.
arxiv-2601-19802:
Aohua Li and four colleagues tackle stance detection, the task of telling whether a text supports or opposes a target. Classic systems are given the target in advance. On real social media, targets are not fixed. They appear, shift, and multiply as events unfold.

The authors propose a new task: zero-shot stance detection in the wild. Their approach generates candidate targets dynamically from the text itself. It then adapts to several targets at once. Systems built this way could track public opinion during breaking events without retraining. The work moves stance detection from the lab toward the mess of live platforms.
arxiv-2601-20002:
Mary Anne Limbach and colleagues describe how a future telescope could find moons around distant giant planets. Giant planets in the habitable zone might host moons with conditions suitable for life. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is a planned space telescope that could search for them. The authors focus on one detection method: lunar eclipses in reflected light.

When a moon passes into its planet's shadow, its reflected light briefly vanishes. That dip is a broadband eclipse signature the observatory could catch. Repeating eclipses would confirm a moon on an orbit. Finding an Earth-like moon, an Endor in their playful framing, is a long-term goal of exoplanet science. The paper works out whether this eclipse route is practical.
arxiv-2601-20102:
Amirhossein Haji Mohammad Rezaei and Zahra Shakeri test whether irrelevant cultural cues can derail medical AI. A medical language model should not change a correct diagnosis because a question mentions the patient's culture. Yet culture-related tokens might bias its reasoning. The authors build a counterfactual benchmark to measure the effect cleanly.

They expand a set of medical exam questions into many variants. Variants insert cultural identifiers, contextual cues, or both, for three patient groups. Comparing accuracy across variants isolates whether identifiers or context do the damage. Equitable healthcare needs models robust to such non-decisive information. The benchmark gives developers a concrete fairness test for medical question answering.
arxiv-2601-20202:
Sasha Levina and six colleagues link cosmic star formation history to the black hole mergers that gravity-wave detectors observe. Mergers of binary black holes offer a window into the lives of massive stars across cosmic time. To read that window, models must know how fast stars formed and how rich in heavy elements the gas was at each era.

The authors test what happens when simple analytical star formation histories stand in for full cosmological simulations. Their question is how much that shortcut shifts the predicted merger population. Getting this right matters for turning detector counts into a history of massive stars.
arxiv-2601-20302:
Suresh Das, Siladittya Manna, and Sayantari Ghosh improve bladder segmentation in CT-guided brachytherapy, a treatment that places radiation sources near a tumor. Outlining the bladder well is essential for giving the right dose and sparing healthy organs. Deep models lose accuracy when the scan distribution shifts, a problem known as covariate shift.

The authors ask whether samples from one distribution can aid learning on a shifted one. Their answer is a data-doping approach with dual-domain learning. Better outlines under shift would make dose plans safer for patients whose scans differ from the training set.
arxiv-2601-20402:
Ananya Shukla, Chaitanya Modi, Satvik Bajpai, and Siddharth Siddharth present GuideAI, a real-time personalized learning system. Large language models are strong learning tools, but they cannot sense a learner's cognitive or physiological state. Existing adaptive systems trace knowledge and test generically, yet miss real-time signals like cognitive load, attention shifts, and engagement.

GuideAI adds adaptive interventions driven by those live signals. The system aims to adjust help as the learner's state changes, not just as answers come in. Learning support that responds to overload or drift could help students stick with hard material longer.
arxiv-2601-20502:
Nathanaël Enriquez, Mike Liu, Laurent Ménard, and Vianney Perchet study optimal matching under size priority in edge-weighted random graphs. Earlier work on the local limit of maximal weight matchings assumed the weights are atomless, which guarantees a unique best matching. That assumption excludes maximal size matchings, where all edge weights are equal.

The authors overcome the difficulty by assigning independent random weights as tiebreakers. Matching problems sit beneath assignment markets, from jobs to kidneys. Handling the equal-weight case extends the theory to the setting where sheer size, not weight, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-18602:
Daniel Neuen and Tim Seppelt ask how few kinds of test graphs one needs to tell two graphs apart. A famed claim says two graphs are the same in form if and only if each test graph sends the same count of maps into both. That claim needs all test graphs at once, which is a huge set. Work since then asks if thin sets of test graphs can do the same job.

The pair look at sparse test graphs, ones with few links for their size. Sparse tests are cheap to count, so a thin set that still tells graphs apart would be a win. Their work maps which graph pairs sparse tests can split and which they blur. That map feeds the maths of graph form, a base for checks on nets and on code that sorts them.
arxiv-2601-18702:
Hansheng Ren argues that deep learn tools trade truth of counts for speed, and that the trade caps what they can think. Most tools store counts with a set count of bits. That cap makes sums drift as chains of steps grow long. Ren claims that high thought, in which one step rests on the last with care, needs counts with no set cap.

He sets out a frame, named Halo, built on exact whole counts with no cap on size. Such counts never drift, no chain is too long. The frame aims to let a tool think in long, exact chains that float counts would foul. The claim is bold and far from proved in use. Read it as a call to weigh truth of counts as a first need, not as a cost to trim.
arxiv-2601-21502:
Yiteng Zhang, Li-Ping Yang, Hong-Hao Tu, and Yueshui Zhang compute small-size corrections in the two-dimensional Ising model. The Ising model is a basic model of magnetism on a grid. The quantity at hand, the crosscap overlap, links the model to questions in topology and quantum field theory.

The authors work along the model's self-dual critical line, where the physics is richest. They rewrite the overlap with a fermion method and use contour integrals to extract the corrections. Precise corrections matter because finite grids are what computers and experiments actually handle. The results sharpen tests of theory against simulation.
arxiv-2601-21702:
Tien Dang and seven co-authors show that unlearning in language models can steer behavior in chosen directions, not just erase it. One family of methods forgets by redirecting the inner representations of the items to forget. The target vectors used for that redirection have been little studied.

Viewed through the lens of linear representations, those targets do more than delete. They can elicit side behaviors and even new capabilities in a controlled way. That finding cuts both ways: unlearning tools are also steering tools. Teams using them to comply with deletion duties should know they may be tuning the model's behavior at the same time.
arxiv-2601-22602:
Zhigang Bao, Kha Man Cheong, Yuji Li, and Jiaxin Qiu watch for sudden shifts in the covariance of a data stream, live. Covariance tracks how variables move together; a break in it can flag a regime change. Their 2026 preprint notes that most past work hunts breaks in stored, past data, even in high dimensions.

Online detection must call the break as it happens. Their spectral method reads the stream's eigen-shape for that call. Fast flags serve finance, sensors, and network watch. The work brings a stored-data art into real time. That move is the contribution.
arxiv-2601-22702:
Katinka Becker and a team built Metric Hub, a library and workflow for picking data quality metrics in medical AI. ML tools now aid therapy choice, ward watch, and treatment. Their 2026 preprint notes that trust needs proof. Doctors, patients, and regulators all ask for it. Proof, in turn, needs the right metrics for the use at hand.

The hub helps teams pick metrics by use case, not by habit. A shared library ends the scatter of local lists. The work is infrastructure for safe medical AI. It makes quality claims easier to check. Good metrics are a quiet kind of safety.
arxiv-2601-21802:
Hoang Khang Phan and co-authors address a risky nursing skill: endotracheal suctioning, which clears a patient's airway through a tube. The procedure is essential but invasive, and it takes real skill to keep patient risk low. In home care and training settings, expert supervision is often limited.

Their 2026 preprint presents a unified approach that pairs explainable artificial intelligence with a large language model to recognize suctioning activity. A system that can spot the steps of the procedure, and explain its judgments, could give trainees feedback when no instructor is present. That kind of support could make practice safer and more consistent for a procedure where small errors carry real weight.
arxiv-2601-21902:
Jonas Möller, Erik Imgrund, Thorsten Eisenhofer, and Konrad Rieck show that computer hardware itself can hide a trap. Machine learning models run on many kinds of hardware, which is expected to give identical results. In practice, design differences cause small numerical variations during inference.

The team shows those tiny variations can be exploited to create backdoors: hidden triggers that change a model's behavior only on certain hardware. Their 2026 preprint calls these hardware-triggered backdoors. The finding matters for security audits, because a model could pass every test on one machine and misbehave on another. It also raises hard questions about how to certify models that will run on chips the tester does not control.
arxiv-2601-22002:
Anderson de Andrade, Alon Harell, and Ivan Bajić squeeze Transformer inference across multiple devices. Transformers perform superbly, but they demand heavy compute and memory while running. Splitting inference across devices can help, yet the split requires compressing the intermediate representations passed between devices.

That compression is a rate-distortion problem: spend few bits, lose little quality. The team's 2026 preprint applies rate-distortion optimization to decide how those internal activations should be compressed. Done well, split inference lets large models run on clusters of modest hardware, cutting cost and energy. It also helps privacy-sensitive setups where no single machine should hold, or handle, the whole computation.
arxiv-2601-20802:
Jonas Hübotter and a large team of co-authors rethink how language models learn from rewards. Their 2026 paper studies reinforcement learning in domains where answers can be checked, like code and math. Current methods learn from one scalar reward per attempt. The authors call that a severe bottleneck for credit assignment. A single number cannot say which step helped.

Their answer is reinforcement learning via self-distillation. In distillation, one model teaches another; here the model teaches itself. The idea is to draw richer signals from the model's own attempts. That way, credit can flow to the steps that earned it. The paper speaks to the push for models that reason better without costly human labels. It targets a weak point in how such training now works.
arxiv-2601-20902:
Katy Chubb makes the case for polarimetry in the study of planets beyond our solar system. The 2026 paper looks ahead to NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory, or HWO. JWST has recently succeeded in reading exoplanet atmospheres. The upcoming Ariel mission will extend that work. HWO is planned as the next breakthrough in atmosphere characterisation. The UK has a strong presence in both the instrument and science work.

Polarimetry measures how light waves align after touching a planet. That signal carries news about atmospheres, clouds, and surfaces. It can reveal traits that plain spectra miss. Chubb argues this tool deserves a central role in HWO's design. The paper is a science case, written to shape a future flagship mission. It speaks to planners who decide what the next great observatory will measure.
arxiv-2601-21002:
Rakesh k Jha traces four roads to the same thermal destination in quantum field theory. The 2026 paper studies inequivalent purifications of the Rindler wedge. The Rindler wedge is the region of spacetime seen by a uniformly accelerating observer. The Minkowski vacuum, restricted to that wedge, looks thermal. Jha builds a hierarchy of null-shifted Rindler wedges to probe that fact. Several transformation paths connect the frames.

The paths include direct Minkowski-to-Rindler mappings. They also include spatial translations and sequential null displacements. Each path yields its own Bogoliubov transformation and particle content. Comparing them shows which thermal features are robust. The fourfold path of the title is that comparison. The work serves theorists of horizons and the Unruh effect. It clarifies how observer motion manufactures heat from emptiness.
arxiv-2601-21102:
S M Mahedy Hasan, Md Fazle Rabbi, and Minhaz Zibran study code contributions that arrive without a word. Their 2026 paper examines AI-generated silent pull requests. A pull request proposes changes to a software project. Silent ones carry no comments or discussions at all. This is the first empirical study of such contributions, the authors report. The silence poses a unique challenge. Reviewers cannot see the rationale behind the code.

Without discussion, acceptance and rejection look arbitrary. The study asks what happens to these quiet contributions. It traces whether they merge, stall, or die. The findings matter as AI writes more of the world's code. Maintainers need norms for work that cannot explain itself. The paper gives the community its first counted look at the phenomenon.
arxiv-2512-01502:
Dennis Gross studies how to verify policies learned by quantum reinforcement learning. Such policies use quantum traits to pick actions in sequence. They aim to beat classic policies on some tasks. But quantum hardware adds noise from measures and flaws.

That noise makes a policy's acts less sure. Gross works on formal checks that hold under that noise. A checked policy can be trusted to meet set bounds. Trust matters if quantum agents are to run in labs or plants where a bad act has a real cost. Noise-aware checks also state plainly what they cannot promise, so users know which policy acts stay open to hardware drift over time.
arxiv-2512-01702:
Bei Zhou and co-authors map heart activation fast across many atrial shapes. Maps of electrical activation guide treatment of arrhythmias. Detailed simulations are too slow for clinic use or large cohorts. Each heart's shape differs, which breaks fixed-grid methods.

Their operator-learning frame ignores the specific geometry. It predicts local activation time fields almost at once. One trained model serves diverse left atrial shapes. Near-instant maps could let doctors test ablation plans live, tuned to each patient's own heart shape. Near-instant maps also scale to cohorts, letting trials compare activation patterns across hundreds of patients in the time one simulation once took.
arxiv-2601-22902:
Michał Marczenko and Krzysztof Redlich look inside baryons, the heavy particles made of quarks, for a hidden pairing. They study how conserved charges fluctuate in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. Their model treats mesons and baryons as open strings with different ends.

Mesons end in a quark and an antiquark, while baryons end in a quark and a paired diquark. That picture yields a fast-growing spectrum of states with a limiting temperature set by string tension. Charge fluctuations then become a test for whether the diquark picture is right.
arxiv-2601-23002:
Cheng Ma and a large team extend a fast theory for matter under extreme heat and pressure. Orbital-free density functional theory can explore electronic structure where experiments are hard. New X-ray laser tools can now probe such states directly, in settings like star interiors and fusion experiments.

That progress challenges theory to match what the lasers measure. The authors push the orbital-free approach to unlock wider exploration of extreme matter. Better theory helps interpret fusion shots and models of planets and stars. X-ray free-electron laser diagnostics motivate the theory, because interpreting those measurements demands models that work at extreme conditions.
arxiv-2601-23102:
Keke Tang and a team of co-authors rethink attacks on three-dimensional point cloud models. Adversarial attacks tweak inputs to fool a model, and transferable ones work on models they never saw. Existing attacks lean on one model's gradients or ad hoc tricks, so they generalize poorly.

Their CoSA framework works inside a compact, shared semantic subspace instead. Perturbations built in that shared space should fool many architectures at once. The study exposes a broad weakness in 3D perception used by robots and self-driving cars. A shared low-dimensional semantic space is the chosen battleground, because features shared across architectures are what make attacks transfer.
arxiv-2512-00002:
Tingyen Wang gauges how much firms in one industry differ from each other. The usual way to fit production models rests on tight preset forms. Those forms can miss how firms act when outcomes are unsure. His framework swaps in a maximum entropy fit, which assumes less, plus a shape-based way to sum up the spread.

Entropy here means the fit uses only what the data support, and no more. The shape tool, called a zonotope, turns the spread of firm traits into a form that can be measured. The work draws on Enterprise Surveys, a large set of firm-level data, so the spread it reports rests on real firms, not stylized ones.
arxiv-2512-00102:
Ahmad Al-Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, and İzzet Sakallı study a black hole surrounded by a cloud of strings in a 2025 study. The black hole is of Letelier type, static and spherically symmetric, and it sits inside an electromagnetic universe. Both surroundings can distort its basic properties.

By deriving the event horizon from the lapse function, the authors show how the string cloud and the electromagnetic background each change the horizon radius. The comparison case is the standard Schwarzschild black hole. Such exact solutions help theorists test how exotic environments would alter the simplest black hole picture. Clouds of strings are an exotic ingredient from early-universe and string-inspired models.
arxiv-2512-00402:
Fuzzy dark matter imagines dark matter as ultralight scalar particles with wave-like behavior. Hayato Shimabukuro, Shihang Liu, and Bohua Li probe its imprint on the cosmic twenty-one centimeter signal in 2025. They use the wavelet scattering transform to read the signal.

Quantum pressure in fuzzy dark matter suppresses small-scale structure, delaying star formation and altering the thermal history of intergalactic gas. Those changes should show in the signal from cosmic dawn and the epoch of reionization. Detecting or ruling out such imprints would narrow what dark matter can be, using radio telescopes as particle detectors. The twenty-one centimeter line comes from hydrogen, the universe's most common element.
arxiv-2512-00502:
The CMS Collaboration reports a first observation of electroweak production of a photon with two forward jets in 2025. The measurement uses proton-proton collision data recorded at the Large Hadron Collider during 2016 to 2018. The collisions ran at the collider's standard high energy.

Electroweak production is rarer and cleaner than the strong-force processes that usually accompany photons and jets. Observing it confirms a predicted corner of the Standard Model and sharpens tools for hunting deviations. Forward jets are a signature of the exchange of weak bosons, so this channel tests electroweak theory in a distinctive regime. The data set is large, which the rare electroweak process requires to be seen at all.
arxiv-2512-03102:
Early guesses in a crisis shape all later choices. Yiwei Shi, Hongnan Ma, Mengyue Yang, Cunjia Liu, and Weiru Liu study how to fix wrong early estimates in this 2025 work. First reports may rest on thin or biased facts, yet plans build on them fast.

Wrong estimates can cause delays, wasted resources, and even harm. The authors propose a method that uses diffusion models to explore and correct the state estimate. Better correction tools could help emergency teams adjust as real facts arrive. The ideas may also serve other high-stakes fields. The method aims to explore better states rather than defend a flawed first guess.
arxiv-2512-03302:
Some particle decays would break a rule thought to be strict. Arindam Das, Takaaki Nomura, and Kei Yagyu study lepton number violation in this 2025 work. They look at decays of the Higgs and Z bosons into pairs of right-handed neutrinos.

Because these neutrinos are Majorana particles, their own antiparticles, the final state can hold same-sign leptons plus jets. That pattern would show two units of lepton number violation. Seeing it would reshape neutrino physics. The authors map where experiments could look for the signal. Same-sign leptons stand out in detectors, since few standard processes produce them.
arxiv-2512-03402:
Fine-tuning large models cheaply is a major goal in AI. Yixing Xu and co-authors present Dual LoRA in this 2025 work. LoRA adapts a model with low-rank updates, but that low-rank limit can hurt performance.

The authors split updates into magnitude and direction parts. Treating those two aspects separately can sharpen adaptation within the same budget. Better parameter-efficient methods let smaller teams customize big models. That lowers cost and energy use while keeping quality high for specific tasks. Splitting magnitude from direction mirrors how vectors change, giving updates more freedom within a small rank budget.
arxiv-2512-02202:
Atomic clocks count the shakes of atoms to keep time. Quantum links between atoms can make those counts sharper than any classic method. Raphael Kaubruegger and Adam Kaufman wrote a 2025 chapter on this linked kind of measure. They show what it can do for optical atomic clocks.

When atoms are linked, a joint measure can beat the noise floor of lone measures. Used in a clock, that means finer timekeeping. Finer clocks aid guidance, earth science, and deep tests of physics. The chapter lays out the core ideas and where they may lead, in the field's most grown-up test bed.
arxiv-2512-02402:
Story generators built on language models often drift from what the user asked, because intent is hard to pin down and controls are coarse. Yunchao Wang and six co-authors present TaleFrame in 2025, an interactive story generation system designed to give users fine-grained control.

The system translates user intent into story outputs more faithfully by clarifying input specifications and exposing detailed levers over the narrative. Creative writing tools live or die by whether the author feels obeyed. TaleFrame's design study shows how much control is enough for generated stories to feel authored rather than merely produced.
arxiv-2512-02502:
Luyao Niu and five co-authors design an app that helps people learn their own neighborhood. The 15-minute city idea holds that daily needs should sit within a short walk or bike ride. Living that way takes more than near shops; people also need fast, reliable facts about nearby places.

AskNearby uses a large language model to answer questions about local services and events. It also builds personalized cognitive map suggestions, tuned to how each person pictures the area. Better local knowledge could help residents actually use what their neighborhood already offers, instead of driving farther by habit. The app fits best in dense towns, where most daily needs sit a short walk from home.
arxiv-2512-02902:
Weiqi Li and four co-authors show that vision language action models generalize better than their failures suggest. Such models drive robots by joining sight, words, and action. They perform strongly in distribution, but degrade sharply under new camera viewpoints and visual changes.

The team traces the brittleness to spatial modeling misalignment, not physical modeling. Their one shot adaptation recalibrates visual representations with lightweight, learnable updates. A tiny fix for spatial alignment could make robot policies far more portable across cameras and rooms, without retraining the whole model. One quick fix that saves a whole rig from scrap is the kind of gain shops dream of when fleets must roll each day.
arxiv-2512-03002:
Proton bunches squeezed to extreme density are a critical step toward future proton driven muon colliders. Compressing a high intensity bunch lengthwise fights the bunch's own space charge, which pushes it apart. The proposed test uses the Integrable Optics Test Accelerator ring at Fermilab.

The experiment would search for the best radio frequency cavity parameters and lattice configurations for compression. Results from a real ring beat pure simulation for such unstable beams. A working compression recipe feeds directly into collider designs that need short, dense proton pulses to make muons. Short dense pops of protons are the feed stock of muon beams. A ring test that finds the best squeeze earns its beam time back in kind.
plos-pone-0010002:
The authors were Feng Wang, Ruixue Zhang, Xiaomeng Wu, and others. Their 2010 study looked at gene control. It asked how low oxygen switches on the erythropoietin gene. That gene makes a hormone that tells the body to build more red blood cells. In the liver cell line they used, a factor called HIF-2 alpha drives most of that switch.

The team tested helper proteins called coactivators, including p300, CBP, and the p160 family. They asked whether these helpers boost the gene's response when oxygen falls and cells need more red blood cells. Knowing the full cast of helpers can guide drugs for anemia and other low-oxygen states.
plos-pone-0010202:
Piwen Wang, Susanne Henning, and David Heber warned about a lab test flaw in 2010. Green tea compounds, called polyphenols, can slow cancer cell growth in dishes. One compound, EGCG, is the most studied of them. Published studies, though, report a wide range of doses needed to halve cell growth in culture.

The team showed that two common assays, MTT and MTS, have limits with these compounds. The tests themselves can distort the readings for green tea polyphenols. Their PLOS ONE warning helps explain the scattered results and pushes labs to check tea findings with other methods.
plos-pone-0009902:
A gene that digests tissue scaffolding is itself controlled differently by each DNA variant. Veronika Souslova and colleagues traced that allele-specific control in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The gene makes matrix metalloproteinase-3, an enzyme tied to arthritis and healing.

Allele-specific regulation means one copy of a gene behaves differently from its twin copy. The control came from NF-kappa-B, a transcription factor that switches genes on during inflammation. Small DNA differences changed how strongly that factor acted. Such details explain why the same gene can raise risk in one person and not another.
